nations.name: Afar
nations.lands: the Afar region of north-eastern Ethiopia, the Dankalia coast of Eritrea, and Djibouti

facts.text: In 2008 Afar pastoralists set up the Afar Pastoralist Council so they could raise their voices at regional, national and international level.

source.title: Afar Pastoralist Council holds Inaugural General Meeting

facts.text: Ethiopia's Afar State is home to about 1.8 million Afar people, by a government projection.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Eritrea chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Anywaa
nations.lands: Gambella in western Ethiopia, along the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers, and neighbouring South Sudan

facts.text: Anywaa activists helped found EMIPRO in 2022, the first legally registered Indigenous-led rights organization in Ethiopia.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

facts.text: The Anywaa are river farmers and fishers whose lives follow the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers of Gambella.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

nations.name: BaAka
nations.lands: forests between the Oubangui and Sangha rivers, in south-western Central African Republic and northern Republic of the Congo

facts.text: Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas credits BaAka knowledge of the forest as central to its research, conservation and tourism work.
The Central African Republic, home to many BaAka communities, ratified ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous peoples in 2010, the first African state to do so.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2021: Central African Republic
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Bagyeli
nations.lands: the forests of southern Cameroon, around Akom II, Bipindi, Kribi and Lolodorf

facts.text: In late 2018 Bagyeli communities filed three Community Forest applications with Cameroon's forestry ministry, after mapping their own forest use.

source.title: Secure land tenure: The legal battles of the Bagyeli

facts.text: Bagyeli and Bakola communities live across about 12,000 km2 of southern Cameroon, especially around Akom II, Bipindi, Kribi and Lolodorf.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Cameroon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Baka
nations.lands: forests of eastern and southern Cameroon, northern Gabon, and neighbouring parts of the Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic

facts.text: In Gabon, the Baka are one of nine Indigenous forest peoples, alongside the Babongo, Bakoya and others, each with its own language and culture.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Gabon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2025 a Batouri workshop run by the association ASBABUK and Cameroon's forestry ministry focused on fully recognizing Baka as rightful partners in managing forest resources.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Cameroon
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Batwa
nations.lands: south-western Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

facts.text: In Burundi, Batwa have been represented in the country's main decision-making bodies since 2005.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2023: Burundi
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2021 Uganda's Constitutional Court found that Batwa were evicted from ancestral lands without consent and sent the question of compensation to a lower court.

source.title: MRG welcomes Uganda court verdict on Batwa compensation

nations.name: Benet
nations.lands: the slopes of Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda, in Kween, Kapchorwa and Bukwo districts

facts.text: In May 2023 Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister directed the wildlife authority (UWA) to stop evictions of Benet communities.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Uganda chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2005 Uganda's High Court recognized the Benet as the historical, indigenous inhabitants of Mount Elgon, a landmark land-rights ruling.

source.title: Momentous Ruling Recognizes Land Rights of Indigenous Community

nations.name: Datooga
nations.lands: northern Tanzania, including the highlands near Mount Hanang in Manyara Region and the Lake Eyasi area

facts.text: Datooga and Hadza communities own more than 110,000 hectares of dryland forest protected through the Yaeda-Eyasi Landscape project.
With help from the NGO Ujamaa Community Resource Team, Barabaig communities in northern Tanzania gained grazing land held under collective title.

nations.name: Endorois
nations.lands: around Lake Bogoria in Baringo County, and in Nakuru and Laikipia counties, in Kenya's Rift Valley

facts.text: The Endorois Welfare Council, founded in 1995 by senior members of the community, works for justice and sustainable development for the Endorois.

source.title: Endorois Welfare Council - Endorois Welfare Council for marginalized communities

facts.text: In 2010 the African Union approved an African Commission ruling in the Endorois case, the first in Africa to recognize Indigenous peoples' rights to land they traditionally owned.

source.title: Landmark decision rules Kenya’s removal of indigenous people from ancestral land illegal

nations.name: Griqua
nations.lands: the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa

facts.text: Griqua communities live today in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Early Griqua communities governed themselves through leaders called kaptyns, with magistrates drawn from leading families.

nations.name: Hadzabe
nations.lands: the hills and valleys around Lake Eyasi in northern Tanzania

facts.text: Hadzabe communities are calling for community-led tourism that ensures transparency, dignity and a fair share of the benefits.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Tanzania
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Hadza people speak Hadzane, a language isolate, which means it is not related to any other known language.

nations.name: Hai//om
nations.lands: north-central Namibia, in and around Etosha National Park and on resettlement farms in Kunene, Oshikoto and Oshana regions

facts.text: In July 2026 Namibia's Vice President opened a high-level meeting in Outjo with the Hai//om Traditional Authority on a development plan for Hai//om communities.

source.title: Government Reaffirms Commitment to Hai-//om Community Development, Vice President Lucia Witbooi (speech)

facts.text: Many Hai//om communities lived on lands that are now Etosha National Park and the surrounding regions, according to the Hai//om Community San Council.

source.title: Challenges Faced by the Hai//om San Marginalized Communities in Namibia: Challenges and Solutions
source.publisher: Cultural Survival (by the Hai//om Community San Council)

nations.name: Imazighen
nations.lands: North Africa (Tamazgha): Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt's Siwa oasis, with communities across the Sahel and in the diaspora

facts.text: Amazigh identity and the Amazigh language, Tamazight, have had official recognition in Morocco's Constitution since 2011.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Morocco
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: After decades of campaigning, Tamazight was recognized as a national and official language in Algeria's Constitution in 2016.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Algeria
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Ishelhiyen
nations.lands: the Souss valley, the Anti-Atlas and the western High Atlas of south-western Morocco

facts.text: In the Souss-Massa region, 63.2% of residents use Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin, according to Morocco's 2024 census.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Souss-Massa
source.publisher: Haut-Commissariat au Plan (HCP), Direction Régionale de Souss Massa

facts.text: Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin of southern Morocco, is one of three Amazigh languages taught at Inalco in Paris.

source.title: Kabyle (Berber)
source.publisher: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)

nations.name: Ju|'hoansi
nations.lands: Nyae Nyae and the Tsumkwe area of north-eastern Namibia, and neighbouring north-western Botswana

facts.text: When Ju|'hoansi formed their farmers' cooperative, they began with open consensus meetings, then elected two representatives per community, at least one of them a woman.

source.title: Controlling Their Destiny: Ju|'hoansi of Nyae Nyae

facts.text: Ju|'hoansi is the one San language Namibia has approved for teaching in schools, but a 2025 review of 14 schools found it is seldom used in class.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Namibia
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Kabyles
nations.lands: Kabylia in north-eastern Algeria, with a large community in France

facts.text: Taqbaylit, the Kabyle language, is one of three Amazigh languages taught from bachelor's level to doctorate at Inalco in Paris.

source.title: Kabyle (Berber)
source.publisher: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)

facts.text: Kabyles make up around half of Algeria's Amazigh population, centred on Kabylia in the north-east.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Algeria chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Karimojong
nations.lands: the Karamoja drylands of north-eastern Uganda

facts.text: The Karimojong, whose economy has long rested on livestock, live mainly in the drylands of north-eastern Uganda, about 1.09 million people in a 2018 estimate.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Uganda chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Cultural Heritage Clubs in five secondary schools in Napak and Moroto treat heritage as central to Karimojong history and identity.

source.title: Karamoja Cultural Heritage Education Programme
source.publisher: Kara-Tunga (partner of Cross Cultural Foundation Uganda)

nations.name: Kel Tamasheq
nations.lands: the Sahara and Sahel: northern Mali and Niger, southern Algeria and Libya, and northern Burkina Faso

facts.text: In Libya, the Fezzan region, including Ubari and Ghat, is traditional Kel Tamasheq territory, linked to communities across the borders in Niger and Algeria.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Libya
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In Niger, Kel Tamasheq (Tuareg) herders raise camels and goats in Agadez, Tahoua and Tillabéry. Estimates for 2009 put them at about 1.2 million, 8.3% of the population.

source.title: Indigenous World 2020: Niger
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Khoikhoi
nations.lands: South Africa, especially the Western, Northern and Eastern Cape, including Nama, Griqua and Korana communities

facts.text: Rooibos benefit money now helps fund local schools, water pumps, student fees and an organic rooibos nursery in Cederberg communities such as Wupperthal.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: South Africa
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Many South Africans once classed as Coloured under apartheid now identify as Khoikhoi or San, exercising their right to self-identification.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Khwe
nations.lands: north-eastern Namibia, north-western Botswana and southern Angola, and Platfontein near Kimberley in South Africa

facts.text: In South Africa, Khwe and !Xun communities live mainly at Platfontein, near Kimberley.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Khwe people in Namibia have their own Traditional Authority. As of 2025 the government had not recognized it, which Khwe say makes land and development issues harder to resolve.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Namibia
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Konso
nations.lands: the Konso highlands of south-western Ethiopia

facts.text: The Konso built the dry-stone terraces of their highlands and still farm them; UNESCO lists the Konso Cultural Landscape as World Heritage.
In Konso walled towns, communal spaces called moras keep a central place in community life.

nations.name: Korana
nations.lands: Kimberley and the Free State province, South Africa

facts.text: Korana communities live mainly in Kimberley and in the Free State province.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In their own !Ora language, the Korana's name for themselves is !Orakua or !Orana.

source.title: Kora: A Lost Khoisan Language of the early Cape and the Gariep, Introduction (Menán du Plessis)

nations.name: Maasai
nations.lands: southern Kenya and northern Tanzania, on both sides of the border

facts.text: In 2025 Tanzania's Simanjiro district paused carbon project signings for 30 days to respond to community concerns, which IWGIA read as a sign that communities are starting to be heard.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Tanzania
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Maasai people speak Maa, a Nilotic language related to Dinka, Kalenjin and Nuer.

nations.name: Mbororo
nations.lands: Cameroon, Chad, Nigeria, the Central African Republic and Niger, often along borderland grazing routes

facts.text: Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, a Mbororo woman from Chad who founded the group AFPAT, chaired the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues for its 2024 session.

source.title: Previous Chairpersons of the Permanent Forum
source.publisher: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNPFII)

facts.text: Mbororo pastoralists in Cameroon are estimated at over one million people, living mainly near the borders with Nigeria, Chad and the Central African Republic.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Cameroon
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Mbuti
nations.lands: the Ituri forest of north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

facts.text: A 2022 national law in the DR Congo, in force since February 2023, recognizes the rights of Indigenous peoples, including the Mbuti, to their lands, territories and resources.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: UNESCO calls for ensuring the involvement of the Indigenous Mbuti and Efe peoples in the management of the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

nations.name: Mozabite
nations.lands: the M'Zab valley around Ghardaïa in the Algerian Sahara

facts.text: UNESCO credits the M'Zab with an ingenious system for capturing and sharing water which, with its palm groves, makes life work in a semi-desert.
The M'Zab valley habitat, built in the tenth century by the Ibadites around five ksour (fortified towns), survives intact and is UNESCO World Heritage.

nations.name: Nama
nations.lands: southern Namibia and the Richtersveld and Namaqualand areas of South Africa's Northern Cape, with smaller communities in Botswana

facts.text: In 2003 South Africa's Constitutional Court recognized the Richtersveld Nama community's communal Indigenous right to its land and the resources in it.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: South Africa
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In South Africa's Richtersveld, Nama families still build portable rush-mat houses called haru oms and move herds between seasonal grazing grounds.

nations.name: Naro
nations.lands: Ghanzi District in western Botswana, and eastern Namibia

facts.text: In 2025 Botswana's government started radio programs in a number of Indigenous languages, Naro among them.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Botswana
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Botswana chose Naro, the main San language of Ghanzi District, as one of the mother-tongue languages for primary school teaching from 2022.

source.title: Forty years of fighting for literacy The case of Naro Bible translators

nations.name: Ogiek
nations.lands: highland forests of Kenya, especially the Mau Forest

facts.text: In December 2025 the African Court issued its first ever compliance decision, in the Ogiek case, finding that Kenya had not yet carried out its judgments.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Kenya
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: In 2017 the African Court ruled for the Ogiek, its first ruling for an Indigenous people, and recognized Indigenous peoples as guardians of local ecosystems.

nations.name: Oromo
nations.lands: Oromia and other regions of Ethiopia, and northern Kenya

facts.text: Knowledge of the Gada system is passed on to Oromo children today, at home and at school.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo

facts.text: UNESCO lists the Gada system as an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo, inscribed on its heritage list in 2016.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo

nations.name: Ovahimba
nations.lands: Kunene Region of north-western Namibia and south-western Angola

facts.text: Ovahimba speak a Herero language and keep semi-nomadic herding homelands that reach from north-western Namibia into south-western Angola.
Ovahimba are mainly herders whose homes lie in the dry mountains and plains of north-west Namibia's Kunene Region.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2026: Namibia
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Rifians
nations.lands: the Rif of northern and north-eastern Morocco, including Al Hoceima province

facts.text: In Morocco's 2024 census, 53.6% of people in Al Hoceima province said they use Tarifit, the language of the Irifiyen.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

facts.text: Nationwide, 3.2% of Morocco's population reported Tarifit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

nations.name: Samburu
nations.lands: Samburu County and nearby rangelands of north-central Kenya

facts.text: All of Reteti's elephant keepers come from the Samburu community and are formally trained to care for, rehabilitate and release elephant calves.

source.title: Home | Reteti Elephant Sanctuary in Kenya

facts.text: With support from the Samburu Women's Trust, Samburu women are exercising land rights: 20 women and three women's groups own land in one home area.

source.title: Empowering women means taking a stand for environmental rights

nations.name: Sengwer
nations.lands: Cherangany Hills and Embobut Forest in Kenya's western highlands

facts.text: Sengwer society is organized around clans, each with its own roles, and elders guide decisions and teach younger generations.
Sengwer knowledge includes sustainable ways of hunting, gathering, beekeeping and caring for forest resources, which helps conserve biodiversity.

nations.name: Siwans
nations.lands: the oases of Siwa and El-Gara in Egypt's Western Desert, near the border with Libya

facts.text: A sense of Berber belonging has revived in Siwa this century; a letter of the Tifinagh alphabet, the Amazigh symbol, now names a bazaar below old Shali.

source.title: Siwa, the Berber oasis where cultures cross (An Atlas of Contemporary Egypt, 2023)

facts.text: Ten Siwan tribes speak Siwi, an eastern Amazigh (Berber) language, in the oases of Siwa and El-Gara.

source.title: Siwa, the Berber oasis where cultures cross (An Atlas of Contemporary Egypt, 2023)

nations.name: Toubou
nations.lands: the Tibesti plateau of northern Chad, southern Libya along the Chad border, and northern Niger

facts.text: Toubou herders practise mobile pastoralism across a wide area stretching from northern Niger to Sudan.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: About 50,000 Toubou live in Libya along the border with Chad; the people's origins lie in the Tibesti plateau.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Tshwa
nations.lands: Tsholotsho and Bulilimamangwe districts of western Zimbabwe

facts.text: Zimbabwe's 2013 Constitution lists Koisan among its 16 languages, and in 2023 the Tsoro-o-tso San Development Trust worked on the Tjwao language.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Zimbabwe chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: About 3,207 Tshwa live in Zimbabwe, where they self-identify as an Indigenous people, mostly in the western districts.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Zimbabwe chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Wodaabe
nations.lands: the Sahel of Niger, with communities in Chad, northern Cameroon and north-east Nigeria

facts.text: In 2008 thousands of Wodaabe herders attended the fourth General Assembly of the Woodaabe Pastoralists of Niger.

source.title: Oromo pastoralists visit Woodaabe General Assembly in Niger

facts.text: Cattle herding is the main livelihood of the Wodaabe, who move with the seasons across the Sahel.

nations.name: !Xun
nations.lands: north-eastern Namibia and southern Angola, and Platfontein near Kimberley in South Africa

facts.text: In South Africa, !Xun and Khwe communities live mainly at Platfontein, near Kimberley.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: XK FM, a public station first on air in 2000, now broadcasts from Platfontein about 15 hours a day in the !Xun and Khwe languages.

source.title: MEDIA STATEMENT | SABC CELEBRATES THE HISTORY AND CULTURE OF THE !XU AND KHWE

nations.name: Yiaku
nations.lands: Mukogodo Forest in Laikipia County, Kenya

facts.text: Yiaku women and elders now lead language teaching and forest care, and growing youth involvement is strengthening the community.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

facts.text: Since 2003 the Yiaku Laikipiak Trust has worked to protect Mukogodo Forest and keep Yiaku culture alive.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

nations.name: ǂKhomani
nations.lands: the southern Kalahari in South Africa's Northern Cape, including the Kalahari Gemsbok National Park near the borders with Botswana and Namibia

facts.text: ǂKhomani people have won back cultural rights in South Africa's Kalahari Gemsbok National Park, such as using its resources and hunting in traditional ways across much of it.
The ǂKhomani are actively reclaiming their knowledge and traditions. Their Kalahari homeland became a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2017.

nations.name: Ahtna
nations.lands: Copper River basin and the upper Susitna and Nenana river areas, Alaska, United States

facts.text: Ahtna is the Athabascan language of the Copper River and the upper Susitna and Nenana drainages, home to eight Ahtna communities.

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: A comprehensive Ahtna dictionary was published in 1990, building on language documentation that began in 1973.

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq
nations.lands: Kodiak Archipelago, Alaska Peninsula, outer Kenai Peninsula and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: At the Alutiiq Museum, fluent speakers, learners and linguists work together to record Sugt'stun and teach it to a new generation of speakers.
Sugpiaq, the people's traditional name for themselves, joins suk, meaning person, with piaq, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Alutiiq / Sugpiaq
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: CHamoru
nations.lands: Guam (Guåhan) in the Mariana Islands, a United States territory

facts.text: Guam's Department of Chamorro Affairs works to preserve, develop and promote CHamoru heritage, with a division devoted to language and culture.

source.title: About Us
source.publisher: Department of Chamorro Affairs, Government of Guam

facts.text: Guam's Public Law 12-132 made both English and CHamoru official languages of the island.

source.title: Role of Education in the Preservation of Guam's Indigenous Language

nations.name: Cup'ik
nations.lands: Chevak and the nearby Bering Sea coast of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In Chevak the people and their language are called Cup'ik, and on Nunivak Island the related form is Cup'ig, each used in place of the word Yup'ik.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: Hooper Bay-Chevak is one of the five dialects of the Central Alaskan Yup'ik language.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Deg Hit'an
nations.lands: Shageluk, Anvik and Holy Cross on the lower Yukon River, Alaska, United States

facts.text: Deg Xinag is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
Deg Xinag is the Athabascan language of the Deg Hit'an in Shageluk and Anvik and of the Athabascan community at Holy Cross on the lower Yukon River.

source.title: Languages - Deg Xinag
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Dena'ina
nations.lands: Cook Inlet region of Southcentral Alaska, including the Kenai Peninsula and the Anchorage area, United States

facts.text: The Kenaitze Indian Tribe states its vision as assuring that the Kahtnuht'ana Dena'ina thrive forever.
Dena'ina is the only Alaska Athabascan language spoken in a coastal setting, and the only one spoken on both sides of the Alaska Range.

source.title: Languages - Dena'ina
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Eyak
nations.lands: Cordova, the Copper River Delta and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: The Native Village of Eyak in Cordova is a federally recognized tribe that unites Eyak, Chugach Region, Tlingit and Athabaskan peoples.

source.title: Native Village of Eyak - About Us

facts.text: Eyak is not an Athabascan language but its own branch beside the Athabascan languages, within the Athabascan-Eyak-Tlingit language family.

source.title: Languages - Eyak
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Gwich'in
nations.lands: Northeast Alaska, including Fort Yukon, Venetie and Arctic Village, plus northern Yukon and the Northwest Territories in Canada

facts.text: Dinjii Zhuh K'yaa, the Gwich'in language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
Gwich'in Council International represents about 9,000 Gwich'in in Alaska, Yukon and the Northwest Territories as a Permanent Participant in the Arctic Council.

nations.name: Haida
nations.lands: Southern Prince of Wales Island, including Hydaburg, Kasaan and Craig, and Ketchikan, Southeast Alaska, United States

facts.text: The Organized Village of Kasaan, a Haida tribal government, works to promote, preserve and protect Haida identity and values for its elders and youth.
Kasaan's 'Láa Náay Justice System works to keep the peace and promote wellness by addressing problems through culturally appropriate methods.

nations.name: Hän
nations.lands: Eagle, Alaska, United States, and Dawson, Yukon, Canada, along the upper Yukon River

facts.text: Hän is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
The Hän language is spoken at Eagle in Alaska and at Dawson in Yukon, and language centers on both sides of the border have documented it.

source.title: Languages - Hän
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Iñupiat
nations.lands: Northwest and Arctic Alaska, from Norton Sound to the North Slope and the Canadian border, United States

facts.text: Iñupiaq is taught in colleges, communities, schools and online, and even in immersion classes for young children before kindergarten.
Iḷisaġvik College in Utqiaġvik was founded to teach from an Iñupiaq cultural foundation, and in 2006 it became the first and only federally recognized tribal college in Alaska.

nations.name: Koyukon
nations.lands: Villages along the Koyukuk River and the middle Yukon River, Interior Alaska, United States

facts.text: Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons for Denaakk'e and nine other Doyon region languages; its first courses came out in summer 2019 and are free.
The language name Denaakk'e comes from denaa, meaning people, plus a suffix meaning like, so it literally means like us.

source.title: Languages - Koyukon
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Lower Tanana Dene
nations.lands: Nenana, Minto and the Fairbanks area along the Tanana River, Interior Alaska, United States

facts.text: Benhti Kenaga', the Lower Tanana language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
A pocket dictionary of the Lower Tanana language, which is spoken in Nenana and Minto on the Tanana River, was published in 2009.

source.title: Languages - Tanana
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Native Hawaiians
nations.lands: The Hawaiian Islands (Hawaiʻi), United States

facts.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, approved by Hawaiʻi voters in 1978 to serve Native Hawaiians, is governed by nine trustees elected statewide for four-year terms.
Since a 1978 amendment to the state constitution, Hawaiian and English have both been official languages of the State of Hawaiʻi.

source.title: State Constitution
source.publisher: Legislative Reference Bureau, State of Hawaiʻi

nations.name: Samoans
nations.lands: Tutuila, Aunuʻu and the Manuʻa Islands of American Samoa, a United States territory in the Samoan Islands

facts.text: In American Samoa, land is held communally under the guidance of village chiefs, the matai, and the national park there sits on land leased from local villages.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

facts.text: Fa'asamoa, the Samoan way of life, took shape over many centuries and remains the base of Samoan identity and everyday living.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

nations.name: St. Lawrence Island Yupik
nations.lands: Gambell and Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea, Alaska, United States; close relatives live on the Chukchi Peninsula across the Bering Strait

facts.text: The Alaska Native Language Center reports that children in Gambell and Savoonga learn St. Lawrence Island Yupik as the first language of the home.

source.title: Languages - Siberian Yupik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: St. Lawrence Island Yupik is almost the same language as the one spoken just across the Bering Strait, at the tip of Siberia's Chukchi Peninsula.

source.title: Languages - Siberian Yupik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Tlingit
nations.lands: Coastal Southeast Alaska from Yakutat south to Ketchikan, United States, with citizens living worldwide

facts.text: The Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska is the tribal government for more than 38,000 Tlingit and Haida citizens worldwide.

source.title: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska
source.publisher: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska

facts.text: Sealaska Heritage Institute says young people who learned Lingít and other Southeast Alaska languages, once nearly lost to oppression, now teach them with help from fluent Elders.

nations.name: Tsimshian
nations.lands: Metlakatla on the Annette Islands Reserve, Southeast Alaska, United States; Tsimshian homelands continue in British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Hyaak Foundation in Metlakatla works to keep Sm'algyax, the Tsimshian language, alive and well.
The Metlakatla Indian Community on the Annette Islands holds the only Indian reserve in Alaska.

nations.name: Unangax̂
nations.lands: Aleutian Islands, Pribilof Islands and the western Alaska Peninsula, Alaska, United States

facts.text: Students in APIA's 2025 Unangam Tunuu Summer Language Intensive learned from Unangax̂ Elders, and APIA holds a weekly Unangam Tunuu Community Night in Anchorage.
The name Unangax̂ means person and likely comes from una, a root that refers to the seaside.

source.title: Languages - Unangam Tunuu / Aleut
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Upper Tanana
nations.lands: Northway, Tetlin and Tok in eastern Interior Alaska, United States, with a small community across the border in Canada

facts.text: Née'aaneegn', the Upper Tanana language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
The Upper Tanana people's own name for their language is Nee'aaneegn'.

source.title: Languages - Upper Tanana
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Yup'ik
nations.lands: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and nearby coasts and rivers of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In the Calista Region along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, subsistence hunting, fishing and gathering bind communities together and are part of who people are.
The word Yup'ik names both the language and the people, built from yuk, meaning person, and pik, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: A'uwe
nations.lands: Eastern Mato Grosso, Brazil, in Indigenous lands such as Pimentel Barbosa, Marãiwatsédé, São Marcos and Sangradouro

facts.text: The A'uwe (Xavante) language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.
The Xavante numbered about 22,256 people in 2020.

nations.name: Achuar
nations.lands: Northern Loreto in Peru near the Ecuador border, and the neighboring Amazon of Ecuador

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture has registered five interpreters and translators of the Achuar language.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: Achuar is a cross-border language, spoken in both Peru and Ecuador.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Ashaninka
nations.lands: Upper Juruá region of Acre, Brazil, including the Amônia, Breu and Envira rivers, near the Peruvian border

facts.text: Ashaninka of the Amônia river created their own association, Apiwtxa, in 1991; it was officially registered in 1993.
Ashenĩka, the people's own name, can be translated as my relatives, my folk or my people.

nations.name: Asháninka
nations.lands: Central Peruvian Amazon in Junín, Ucayali, Pasco, Cusco, Huánuco and Ayacucho

facts.text: In 2017, 73,567 people in Peru said Ashaninka was the language they learned to speak as children.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 55,493 people identified as part of the Asháninka people.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Avá Guarani
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná in Brazil, and eastern Paraguay

facts.text: Guarani peoples, the Avá Guarani among them, live across a territory that spans regions of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina.
The Avá Guarani, called Ñandeva in Brazil, have a present-day territory that takes in parts of Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Awajún
nations.lands: Northern Peruvian Amazon in Amazonas, Loreto, San Martín, Cajamarca and Ucayali

facts.text: The Federation of Aguaruna Women of the Upper Marañón (FEMAAM), founded in Imaza in 2002, opened the way for Awajún women's political participation.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: The Awajún language belongs to the Jivaroan language family.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Baniwa
nations.lands: Içana river and the Upper Rio Negro in Amazonas, Brazil, and neighboring Colombia and Venezuela

facts.text: The Baniwa speak languages of the Arawak family along the Içana river.
Baniwa communities live where Brazil meets Colombia and Venezuela, along the Içana river in the Upper Rio Negro region.

nations.name: Guarani Kaiowá
nations.lands: Southern Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, and neighboring eastern Paraguay, where the people are known as Paĩ Tavyterã

facts.text: Kaiowá, Ñandeva and Mbya Guarani all speak dialects of Guarani and show strong energy in keeping their language alive.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: Guarani communities today call the places they live tekoha, a word that joins land, forest, fields, water, animals, plants and medicines.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Guarani Mbya
nations.lands: Villages across southern and southeastern Brazil, eastern Paraguay, Misiones province in Argentina, and near Montevideo in Uruguay

facts.text: The Comissão Guarani Yvyrupa, founded in 2006, brings together Guarani collectives in six states of southern and southeastern Brazil.
Mbya Guarani keep their language fully alive, and oral transmission is the most effective way they educate their children.

source.title: Guarani Mbya - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Huni Kuin
nations.lands: Rivers of Acre state in western Brazil, such as the Tarauacá, Jordão and Purus, and the Purus and Curanja rivers in Peru

facts.text: Huni kuin, the name the people use for themselves, means true people, or people with known customs.

source.title: Huni Kuin (Kaxinawá) - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: MAHKU, the Huni Kuin Artists Movement founded in Acre in 2013, painted a large mural across the facade of the Central Pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale.

source.title: Biennale Arte 2024 | MAHKU (Movimento dos Artistas Huni Kuin)

nations.name: Ka'apor
nations.lands: Northern Maranhão, Brazil, in the Alto Turiaçu Indigenous Land

facts.text: Ka'apor communities have had a shared, standard sign language for communicating with deaf members of the community.
Ka'apor is a language of the Tupi-Guarani family.

nations.name: Kuikuro
nations.lands: Upper Xingu, in the Xingu Indigenous Territory, Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Kuikuro remains a living, intact language, used by everyone in all domains except talking with outsiders.
Kuikuro is a southern Carib language.

nations.name: Macuxi
nations.lands: Fields and mountains of northern Roraima, Brazil, between the headwaters of the Branco and Rupununi rivers, extending into Guyana and Venezuela

facts.text: The Conselho Indígena de Roraima, founded in 1990, unites ten peoples including the Macuxi and Wapichana, with 270 of the state's 465 communities as members.
The Macuxi language belongs to the Carib language family.

nations.name: Mẽbêngôkre
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, Brazil, along rivers of the Xingu basin such as the Iriri, Bacajá and Fresco

facts.text: The Associação Floresta Protegida, created in 1998 by Mẽbêngôkre leaders, represents about 3,000 people in 31 villages across three Indigenous lands.
The Mẽbêngôkre language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.

nations.name: Munduruku
nations.lands: Tapajós river basin in Pará, with communities in Amazonas and Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Munduruku of the upper Tapajós created the Pusuru Indigenous Association in 1991 as a formal way to organize their communities.
The Munduruku language belongs to its own Munduruku family within the Tupi language stock.

nations.name: Pataxó
nations.lands: Villages in the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais, Brazil

facts.text: The Pataxó are rebuilding their language, Patxohã, through a major community effort.
Pataxó villages are spread across the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais.

nations.name: Pueblo Originario Kichwa de Sarayaku
nations.lands: Middle Bobonaza river basin, Pastaza province, Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: About 1,500 Kichwa people of Sarayaku live in seven community centers across roughly 135,000 hectares on the Bobonaza river in Pastaza, Ecuador.
Sarayaku has its own statute on image, communication and digital sovereignty, setting free, prior and informed consent rules for visitors, press and researchers.

source.title: Statute of Governance of Image, Communication, and Digital Sovereignty of the Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku

nations.name: Qom
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, especially Chaco, Formosa and Santa Fe provinces, plus communities in Buenos Aires and in Paraguay

facts.text: Qom is one of three Indigenous languages that Argentina's Chaco province declared official alongside Spanish in 2010.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

facts.text: The Qom language is being recovered in universities and in community-run spaces, and children and teenagers are taking it up.

source.title: El wichí y el qom comienzan a ser hablados en la primera infancia y en la adolescencia
source.publisher: Unidiversidad, Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (from Télam)

nations.name: Sápara
nations.lands: Rainforest of Pastaza province in the Ecuadorian Amazon, straddling the border with Peru

facts.text: The Sápara live in a part of the Amazon rainforest that straddles Ecuador and Peru.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

facts.text: Sápara knowledge of the forest shows in their rich vocabulary for plants and animals and in their knowledge of the forest's medicinal plants.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

nations.name: Shipibo-Konibo
nations.lands: Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Loreto and Huánuco in Peru, with an urban community at Cantagallo in Lima

facts.text: Cantagallo, home to Shipibo-Konibo families, is the best known Amazonian Indigenous settlement in metropolitan Lima.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 25,232 people identified as part of the Shipibo-Konibo people.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Shuar
nations.lands: Zamora Chinchipe, Morona Santiago and southern Pastaza provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: In 2022 the Shuar Aratsim Center approved its own Life Plan after participatory community workshops.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

facts.text: The Interprovincial Federation of Shuar Centers (FICSH), founded in 1964, was one of the pioneering Indigenous organizations of the Amazon.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

nations.name: Terena
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul, with communities in Mato Grosso and São Paulo, Brazil

facts.text: Terena people living in cities are concentrated mainly in Campo Grande, and most of them keep strong ties with their reserves.
Farming remains the main productive activity in Terena reserves.

nations.name: Tikuna
nations.lands: Along the upper Solimões (Amazon) river in Amazonas, Brazil, and in neighboring Peru and Colombia

facts.text: Tikuna communities are spread across three countries: Brazil, Peru and Colombia.
Tikuna is a tonal language, considered genetically isolated, with a complex sound system and grammar.

nations.name: Tsimane'
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of the Beni department, Bolivia, mainly along the Maniquí and Apere rivers

facts.text: Tsimane' livelihoods center on small farms of plantains, rice, corn and sweet manioc, along with fishing, hunting and gathering.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

facts.text: Almost all Tsimane' speak their own Tsimane' language as their main language.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

nations.name: Tupinambá
nations.lands: Atlantic Forest of southern Bahia around Olivença, in Ilhéus, Buerarema and Una, with Tupinambá communities also in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: The Tupinambá of Olivença live in the Atlantic Forest region of southern Bahia.
In 2001 Funai, Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, officially recognized the Tupinambá of Olivença as an Indigenous people.

nations.name: Waorani
nations.lands: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: Waorani territory includes 32 communities in three Amazonian provinces of Ecuador: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo.
The legally recognized Waorani territory is governed by NAWE, the Waorani Nationality of Ecuador, regarded as the highest Waorani territorial authority.

nations.name: Wapichana
nations.lands: Northeastern Roraima, Brazil, and the South Rupununi in southwestern Guyana

facts.text: In 2012 Wapichan leaders in Guyana presented a community map and land plan titled Thinking Together for those Coming Behind Us.

source.title: Wapichan people in Guyana present territorial map and community proposals to save ancestral forests

facts.text: The Wapichana language is classified in the Arawak language family.

nations.name: Wichí
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, mainly Salta, Formosa and Chaco provinces, with related communities in southern Bolivia

facts.text: In 2010 Argentina's Chaco province made the Wichí, Qom and Moqoit languages official languages of the province alongside Spanish.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

nations.name: Yanomami
nations.lands: Forests of Amazonas and Roraima states in northern Brazil, continuing across the border into southern Venezuela

facts.text: The Yanomami language family is not linked to any other language stock, and it has six languages and sixteen dialects.

source.title: TI Yanomami
source.publisher: Casa Civil da Presidência da República, Governo do Brasil

facts.text: The Yanomami Indigenous Territory in Brazil, about 9.66 million hectares of tropical forest, was ratified by presidential decree on 25 May 1992.

nations.name: Arhuaco
nations.lands: South-eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Cesar and Magdalena, northern Colombia

facts.text: The Confederación Indígena Tayrona, the Arhuaco organization founded in 1976, plans to restore the Guatapurí river basin with 18,000 native trees.
In 2022 UNESCO inscribed the ancestral knowledge system of the Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa peoples as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nations.name: Aymara
nations.lands: The altiplano around Lake Titicaca and nearby valleys and cities of Bolivia and Peru, and the far north of Chile

facts.text: Aymara is a vital language in Peru, where the 2017 census counted 450,010 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

source.title: Aimara | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Bolivia's 2024 census, more than one million people self-identified as Aymara, and more than one million as Quechua.

source.title: INE presenta resultados del Censo 2024 que muestran la transformación demográfica y avances sociales en Bolivia
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística de Bolivia

nations.name: Colla
nations.lands: Atacama Region of Chile, around Copiapó, Chañaral, Tierra Amarilla and Diego de Almagro, and the puna of northwestern Argentina

facts.text: The first Colla Indigenous communities in Chile were officially constituted in the early 1990s.
Colla communities in Chile are found in Atacama Region areas such as Potrerillos and Inca de Oro, in Chañaral, Copiapó and Tierra Amarilla.

nations.name: Diaguita
nations.lands: Huasco and Choapa valleys of Chile's Norte Chico, and northwestern Argentina

facts.text: The first Diaguita community constituted under Chile's Indigenous Law, the Estancia Agrícola Diaguita de los Huascoaltinos, formed in 2006.
Many people who self-identify as Diaguita in Chile live in the upper Huasco River basin, in the municipality of Alto del Carmen.

nations.name: Kággaba
nations.lands: Northern, eastern and western slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Magdalena and Cesar, Colombia

facts.text: The Organización Gonawindúa Tayrona serves as the representative body of the Kággaba people's own Indigenous government.
The Kággaba speak their own language, often called Kogui, which belongs to the Chibcha language family.

source.title: Kaggabba (Kogui): los guardianes de la armonía del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Kankuamo
nations.lands: South-eastern foothills of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta near Valledupar, Cesar, Colombia, centered on Atánquez

facts.text: The Kankuamo resguardo, about 24,212 hectares near Valledupar, was collectively titled to the people in 2003.

source.title: Kankuamos, guardianes del equilibrio del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: In 2022 UNESCO recognized the ancestral knowledge system shared by the Kankuamo, Arhuaco, Kogui and Wiwa as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nations.name: Kichwa
nations.lands: Highland provinces of Ecuador along the Andes, from Imbabura and Pichincha south to Chimborazo, Cañar and Loja

facts.text: Ecuador's Constitution names Kichwa, together with Spanish and Shuar, as official languages of intercultural relations.

source.title: Constitución de la República traducida al kichwa

facts.text: In 2009 Ecuador's Constitution was translated into Kichwa, with five delegates from Indigenous communities reviewing the translation.

source.title: Constitución de la República traducida al kichwa

nations.name: Kichwa Kañari
nations.lands: Cañar and Azuay provinces in the southern highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: The Kañari keep a vigorous ethnic identity and a very strong organizational system, in which cooperatives and many kinds of organizations are very active.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: In Cañar parish, the province's largest Indigenous organizational network brings together 15 communities and 5 cooperatives.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Kichwa Kayambi
nations.lands: Around Cayambe in Pichincha province and neighboring areas of Imbabura, northern Ecuador

facts.text: In 2022 Kayambi water boards, communes and community organizations met with a national legislator to discuss issues including a new water law.

source.title: Asamblea ampliada y mesa de trabajo con el Pueblo Kayambi

facts.text: The Confederación del Pueblo Kayambi holds a General Assembly where its communities and organizations bring their proposals and demands.

source.title: Asamblea General con el Pueblo Kayambi

nations.name: Kichwa Otavalo
nations.lands: Otavalo and nearby communities such as Peguche in Imbabura province, northern Ecuador

facts.text: Hampiriypacha, a Kichwa Otavalo association of seed guardians, works to protect knowledge that women have passed down for generations.

source.title: Meet our 2022 Keepers of the Earth Fund Grant Partners

facts.text: Yarina, a Kichwa Otavalo family band started in 1984, plays original Indigenous rhythms on traditional Andean instruments and works to keep Kichwa traditions alive.

nations.name: Kichwa Puruwá
nations.lands: Chimborazo province in the central highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: The Puruwá people include the communities of Cacha, Colta, Licto and Guamote in Chimborazo, each with its own local character.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: Ecuador's 2010 census counted 136,141 Kichwa Puruwá people, about 18.5 percent of the whole Kichwa nationality.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Kichwa Saraguro
nations.lands: Saraguro canton in Loja province and nearby areas of southern Ecuador

facts.text: In 2019 Radio Kipa, a new community radio station in Saraguro, was one of the few radios to have won a license from Ecuador's state in recent years, and planned to train 30 young people.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: CORPUKIS, a coordinating body of Kichwa Saraguro organizations, works with grassroots groups to advance civil, human and collective rights in its territory.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

nations.name: Lickanantay
nations.lands: Oases and valleys of the Salar de Atacama and the Loa river basin, Antofagasta Region, northern Chile

facts.text: Lickanantay communities are revitalizing their language, Ckunsa. A 2025 regional arts project in Chiu Chiu promotes it through art and stop-motion animation.

source.title: Proyecto Fondart Regional 2025 impulsa la revitalización de la lengua Ckunsa a través del arte y la animación en Chiu Chiu
source.publisher: Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio de Chile

facts.text: Lickanantay communities live in the oases and valleys of the Atacama salt flat and the Loa river basin in Chile's Antofagasta Region.

nations.name: Mapuche
nations.lands: South-central Chile, especially La Araucanía and Santiago, and Patagonian provinces of Argentina such as Neuquén and Río Negro

facts.text: Most Mapuche in Chile today live in cities, with the largest groups in La Araucanía region and in the capital, Santiago.
Mapudungun, the Mapuche language, is still the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Chile.

nations.name: Misak
nations.lands: Resguardos of Guambía and Quisgó in Silvia, Cauca, and nearby municipalities of southwestern Colombia

facts.text: The Misak keep their mother tongue, Wampi-misamerawam, and see it as central to their ethnic and cultural identity.

source.title: Misak (Guambianos), la gente del agua, del conocimiento y de los sueños
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: In 2000 a Misak leader became the first Indigenous person elected by popular vote as governor of Colombia's Cauca department.

source.title: Misak (Guambianos), la gente del agua, del conocimiento y de los sueños
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Nasa
nations.lands: Cauca department, especially Tierradentro and northern Cauca, with communities in Huila, Valle del Cauca, Tolima and Putumayo, Colombia

facts.text: In 1971 Indigenous communities of Cauca founded the CRIC to recover resguardo lands, strengthen their cabildos and defend their history, language and customs.

source.title: Nasa (Paez), la gente del agua
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: The Nasa language is Nasa Yuwe. In Colombia's 2005 census, 41.9 percent of Nasa people reported speaking it.

source.title: Nasa (Paez), la gente del agua
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Pasto
nations.lands: Highlands of Nariño, Colombia, in municipalities such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres, and across the border in northern Ecuador

facts.text: The Pasto are working to recover their identity, oral tradition and ancestral customs, and to strengthen their own law through their cabildos.

source.title: Pastos, los hijos del sol
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Most Pasto communities live in resguardos dating from colonial times and in other lands in Nariño, such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres.

source.title: Pastos, los hijos del sol
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Quechua
nations.lands: Andean highlands and valleys of Peru and Bolivia, with Quechua communities also in Argentina and Chile

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture lists Quechua as a vital language, and the 2017 census counted 3,805,531 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

source.title: Quechuas | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture reports that 5,179,774 people nationwide feel or consider themselves part of the Quechua peoples.

source.title: Quechuas | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Uro
nations.lands: Lake Titicaca, especially the Bay of Puno in Peru, with Uru communities also in Bolivia

facts.text: Uro communities today are working to recover knowledge of their ancestral language, with support from Peru's Ministry of Culture.

source.title: Uro | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: For centuries the Uro have lived on large rafts of totora reed, called floating islands, on Lake Titicaca in the Bay of Puno, and many Uro families still live on them.

source.title: Uro | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Uru Chipaya
nations.lands: Chipaya, on the altiplano of Oruro department, Bolivia

facts.text: The Uru Chipaya nation approved its own autonomy statute by referendum in 2016 and in 2017 became one of Bolivia's first three Indigenous self-governments.

source.title: Charagua, Raqaypampa y Uru Chipaya conforman los primeros tres autogobiernos indígenas de Bolivia
source.publisher: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa

facts.text: Leadership of the Uru Chipaya executive rotates in turns among the nation's four ayllus: Aranzaya, Manazaya, Wistrullani and Ayparavi.

source.title: La rotación de ayllus en el Lanqsñi Paqh mä eph (Órgano Ejecutivo)
source.publisher: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa

nations.name: Wiwa
nations.lands: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Cesar and Magdalena, Colombia

facts.text: Most young Wiwa speak three languages: Damana, their mother tongue, the neighboring Kogui language, and Spanish.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Through education policies the Wiwa established an alphabet for Damana, and they are working to have it taught alongside Spanish in schools.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Yanacona
nations.lands: The Macizo Colombiano in southern Cauca, with communities in Huila and Valle del Cauca, Colombia

facts.text: The Yanacona are recovering their identity and culture, including their traditional language, Quechua, and strengthening their cabildo authorities.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Yanacona territory covers a large part of the Macizo Colombiano, the mountain region of southern Cauca.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Dolgan
nations.lands: Taimyr Peninsula in Krasnoyarsk Krai (Taimyr Dolgan-Nenets District) and the Anabar District and city of Yakutsk in Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Even
nations.lands: Northeastern Siberia: Sakha (Yakutia), Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Khabarovsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: The Even language belongs to the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) branch and is close to Evenki. Even self-names include Even (local) and Orochel (reindeer people).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: The 2002 census counted 11,657 Even living in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Inughuit
nations.lands: Avanersuaq (the Thule region) in northwest Greenland, centred on the town of Qaanaaq

facts.text: Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.
The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.

nations.name: Itelmen
nations.lands: Tigilsky District on the west coast of Kamchatka Krai, with smaller groups in Chukotka and Magadan Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Western Itelmen is the Itelmen language that has been kept to the present day.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Fishing, above all for salmon, is the traditional Itelmen livelihood on Kamchatka.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Kalaallit
nations.lands: Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland), which has self-government within the Kingdom of Denmark

facts.text: Under the Self-Government Act, in force since 21 June 2009, the people of Greenland are recognised as a people with the right to self-determination under international law.
The Self-Government Act recognises Greenlandic (Kalaallisut) as the official language of Greenland.

nations.name: Ket
nations.lands: Yenisei River basin, mainly Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: Ket is the only living language of the Yeniseian language family.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: A Cyrillic writing system that Ket speakers actually use came into being in the late 1980s.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Khanty
nations.lands: River valleys of the Ob basin in western Siberia: Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Tomsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: For many Khanty families, fishing and reindeer herding are closely intertwined, and family fishing hamlets on rivers like the Synia still carry clan surnames.

source.title: Khanty fishing in the Ob' River system, West Siberia, 6 Sep 2023 Rovaniemi talk by Yuka Oishi
source.publisher: Arctic Anthropology blog, Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

facts.text: The first newspaper in the Khanty language in the okrug came out on 1 November 1957. Known today as Khanty Yasang, it is still made by a joint Khanty and Mansi newsroom.

source.title: Историческая справка
source.publisher: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)

nations.name: Koryak
nations.lands: Mainly the north of Kamchatka Krai, Russian Far East

facts.text: In 2000, a Russian government decree gave the Koryak the status of an Indigenous small-numbered people.

source.title: Коряки
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Reindeer herding was the main way of life for nomadic Koryaks, while settled Koryaks mostly fished and hunted sea mammals.

source.title: Коряки
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Luoravetlan
nations.lands: Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, northern Kamchatka Krai and the Nizhnekolymsky District of Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

source.title: Arctic Research Center
source.publisher: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences

facts.text: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

source.title: Чукчи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Mansi
nations.lands: Ob and Irtysh basin in western Siberia, mainly Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), with small groups in Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Luima Seripos, a newspaper in the Mansi language, first came out on 11 February 1989 and is still produced today in a joint newsroom with the Khanty paper.

source.title: Историческая справка
source.publisher: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)

facts.text: Mansi rapper Yevgeny Anyamov, known as Bizzo, records his songs in Mansi and opened his own studio in his hometown of Ivdel to share his people's culture with youth.

nations.name: Nanai
nations.lands: Lower Amur River valley in Khabarovsk Krai and Primorsky Krai, Russia, and the Sungari River area of northeast China

facts.text: Nanai communities also live in China, where about 4,600 Nanai were counted in 2000.

source.title: Нанайцы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Clothing sewn from fish skin is a hallmark of traditional Nanai craft, rooted in a life of fishing on the Amur River.

source.title: Нанайцы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Nenets
nations.lands: Tundra and forest-tundra from the Kola Peninsula to the Yenisei River, including the Nenets and Yamal-Nenets autonomous okrugs and Taimyr, Russia

facts.text: Nenets reindeer herders are regarded today as the most mobile nomads in the world, with large-herd reindeer herding at the heart of the tundra economy.

source.title: Ненцы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: In Yamal, a regional grant helps young Nenets, Khanty and other Indigenous nomadic families with three or more children equip a chum shelter. By 2024, 268 families had received it.

source.title: Young indigenous families supported by chum capital

nations.name: Nganasan
nations.lands: Southern and central Taimyr Peninsula, Krasnoyarsk Krai, including the villages of Ust-Avam, Volochanka and Novaya and the towns of Dudinka and Norilsk, Russia

facts.text: In August 2026, a state folk culture expedition in Taimyr met a knowledge keeper of Vadeyev Nganasan culture, who showed traditional dishes and how Nganasan cuisine differs from Dolgan.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Nganasan belongs to the Samoyedic branch of the Uralic-Yukaghir language family.

source.title: Нганасаны
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Nivkh
nations.lands: Lower Amur River in Khabarovsk Krai and Sakhalin Island, Russia

facts.text: The Nivkh speak a language isolate, probably one of the oldest languages of Eurasia. Its links to other languages have not been established.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Nivkh life was built on fishing and hunting, including sea mammals taken with spears or with nets woven from leather straps.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Odul, Wadul
nations.lands: Kolyma River basin in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) and Magadan Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Today the Yukaghir speak two languages: Northern (Tundra) Yukaghir and Southern (Kolyma) Yukaghir.

source.title: Юкагиры
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: A Cyrillic-based writing system for Yukaghir was developed in the 1970s.

source.title: Юкагиры
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Sámi
nations.lands: Sápmi, across northern Norway, Sweden and Finland and the Kola Peninsula of Russia

facts.text: Norway's Sámi Parliament is elected by and among the Sámi. First opened in Karasjok in 1989, it now has 39 representatives from seven constituencies.
About 10,000 Sámi live in Finland, where three Sámi languages are spoken: Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi.

source.title: About us | The Sámi Parliament of Finland

nations.name: Selkup
nations.lands: Between the middle Ob and Yenisei rivers: the Taz River area of Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and the Narym area of Tomsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Since a 2000 government decree, Russia has listed the Selkup as an Indigenous small-numbered people.

source.title: Селькупы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Selkup belongs to the Samoyedic group of the Uralic language family.

source.title: Селькупы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Udehe
nations.lands: Villages on the Khor and Bikin rivers in Khabarovsk Krai and Primorsky Krai, and towns of both regions, Russia

facts.text: Most Udehe today live in villages on the Khor and Bikin rivers in Russia's Far East.

source.title: Удэгейцы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: The Udehe language belongs to the Amur group of the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) languages.

source.title: Удэгейцы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Yupik
nations.lands: Settlements on the eastern coast of the Chukchi Peninsula, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia, across the Bering Strait from Alaska

facts.text: Inuit from Chukotka became part of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 1992, a goal that was in ICC's vision from the very beginning.
Carving walrus ivory and whale baleen is a highly developed Yupik craft in Chukotka.

source.title: Эскимосы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Ainu
nations.lands: Hokkaido and other parts of Japan

facts.text: Upopoy, a national centre for Ainu history and culture in Shiraoi, Hokkaido, opened to the public in July 2020.

source.title: About Upopoy
source.publisher: Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park

facts.text: A 2019 Japanese law names the Ainu as an Indigenous people of northern Japan, especially Hokkaido, and aims for a society that respects Ainu pride.

source.title: Act on Promoting Measures to Achieve a Society in which the Pride of Ainu People is Respected (Act No. 16 of 2019)
source.publisher: Japanese Law Translation, Ministry of Justice, Japan

nations.name: Akha
nations.lands: Northern Thailand, eastern Myanmar and northern Laos

facts.text: The Akha are one of more than 20 highland Indigenous peoples of northern Thailand.

nations.name: Atayal
nations.lands: Mountain areas of northern and central Taiwan, across New Taipei, Taoyuan, Hsinchu, Miaoli, Taichung, Nantou and Yilan

facts.text: In the Atayal language, the word Atayal means people, real people, or kinspeople.
The Atayal live across the mountains of northern and central Taiwan, the widest spread of any Indigenous people on the island.

nations.name: Bhil
nations.lands: Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra, India

facts.text: India's government names the Bhil among the tribal peoples whose movements strengthened the country's freedom struggle.

source.title: Cabinet approves declaration of 15th November as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas
source.publisher: Prime Minister's Office, Government of India

nations.name: Bodo
nations.lands: Bodoland Territorial Region and other parts of Assam, India

facts.text: Bodo is an associate official language of Assam, and in 2022 the state announced it would become a medium of instruction in Classes XI and XII.

source.title: CM Dr. Sarma attends 61st Annual conference of Bodo Sahitya Sabha (Press Release No. 129/2022)
source.publisher: Directorate of Information and Public Relations, Government of Assam

facts.text: Bodo is one of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution.

source.title: Languages Included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
source.publisher: Department of Official Language, Ministry of Home Affairs, India

nations.name: Bunun
nations.lands: Both sides of the Central Mountain Range in Nantou, Hualien, Taitung and Kaohsiung, Taiwan

facts.text: The Bunun live higher in the mountains than any other Indigenous people in Taiwan, mostly between 500 and 1,500 metres.
About 59,536 Bunun people were counted in January 2020, with homes in Nantou, Hualien, Taitung and Kaohsiung.

nations.name: Chakma
nations.lands: Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh, and parts of northeast India

facts.text: Hill Tracts peoples are sometimes called Jumma, after jum, their traditional method of shifting cultivation.
The Chakma make up more than half of the Indigenous population of Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts.

nations.name: Dayak
nations.lands: Borneo: Kalimantan (Indonesia), Sabah and Sarawak (Malaysia) and Brunei

facts.text: Dayak is a shared name for many Indigenous peoples of Borneo, by some estimates about 450 ethnolinguistic groups.
Dayak peoples share traditions of longhouse living and customary law known as adat.

nations.name: Garo
nations.lands: Garo Hills of Meghalaya, India, and north-central Bangladesh

facts.text: The Garo Hills Autonomous District Council, set up in 1952 under India's Sixth Schedule, is based in Tura and covers five districts.
The Meghalaya government lists Garo among the state's languages, alongside Khasi, Pnar and English.

nations.name: Gond
nations.lands: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Odisha and neighboring states of central India

facts.text: Masaram Gondi, a script created in 1918 by Munshi Mangal Singh Masaram of Madhya Pradesh to write the Gondi language, is still used today in handwritten and printed materials.

source.title: Chapter 13, South and Central Asia-II (The Unicode Standard, Version 18.0)

facts.text: Gond painting, mostly made in Patangarh village in Dindori district, gained worldwide recognition after shows in Tokyo and Paris and became a livelihood for many tribal families.

source.title: Gond Art: Details about Gond Tribal Art and Painting of India
