nations.name: Hla'alua
nations.lands: Taoyuan and Namaxia districts, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan

facts.text: In 2014 the Hla'alua were officially recognized as a distinct people, becoming the 15th Indigenous people listed in Taiwan.
The Hla'alua are formed by four communities, Paiciana, Vilanganʉ, Talicia and Hlihlara, in Kaohsiung City.

nations.name: Ho
nations.lands: Kolhan region of Jharkhand and northern Odisha, with communities in West Bengal and Bihar, India

facts.text: In Odisha, Ho farmers grow paddy, maize and ragi, tend kitchen gardens, and gather mushrooms, mahua and greens from the forest.

source.title: Odisha State Tribal Museum: Ho
source.publisher: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)

facts.text: The Ho language has its own recently devised alphabet, Warang Citi, which is encoded in the Unicode Standard and used by a yearly and a biweekly publication.

source.title: Chapter 13, South and Central Asia-II (The Unicode Standard, Version 18.0)

nations.name: Ibaloi
nations.lands: Southern Benguet and the Baguio area in northern Luzon, Philippines

facts.text: The Ibaloi are one of the three major ethnolinguistic groups of Benguet province, with the Kankanaey and Kalanguya.
Benguet's official provincial fruit is a native blueberry whose Ibaloi name is ayosip.

nations.name: Iban
nations.lands: Sarawak, Malaysia, with communities in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, and Brunei

facts.text: Between 1948 and 1963 the Iban language served as the common language between Sarawak's communities.

source.title: Indigenous peoples and ethnic minorities in Sarawak

facts.text: In 2011 the Tun Jugah Foundation published Bup Sereba Reti Jaku Iban, described as the first monolingual Iban dictionary.

nations.name: Ifugao
nations.lands: Ifugao Province in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, Philippines

facts.text: Ifugao families still farm and care for their mountain rice terraces, a UNESCO World Heritage living landscape since 1995.

source.title: Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras

facts.text: The Hudhud, long narrative chants of the Ifugao sung at rice sowing and harvest, are on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

nations.name: Kadazandusun
nations.lands: Sabah, Malaysia

facts.text: The Kadazan Dusun Cultural Association, founded in 1966, represents 48 Indigenous ethnic communities of Sabah.
KDCA works on preserving, standardizing and developing the Kadazandusun language with its many dialects.

nations.name: Kalasha
nations.lands: The Kalasha valleys of Bamburet, Birir and Rumbur in the Hindu Kush, Chitral, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

facts.text: Kalasha families use Suri Jagek to choose the right time to sow seeds and care for livestock, and to anticipate natural hazards.
Suri Jagek is practiced at local observatories in three Kalasha valley villages: Bamburet, Birir and Rumbur.

source.title: Pakistan's first independent nomination Suri Jagek inscribed by UNESCO (PR No. 04)
source.publisher: Press Information Department, Government of Pakistan

nations.name: Kanakanavu
nations.lands: Namaxia District, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan

facts.text: On June 26, 2014, Taiwan's government recognized the Kanakanavu as an independent people, the 16th on the official list.
Some Kanakanavu people understand their name as people living in a forest of Taiwan giant bamboo.

nations.name: Kankanaey
nations.lands: Benguet and Mountain Province in the Cordillera of northern Luzon, Philippines

facts.text: The Kankanaey are one of the three major ethnolinguistic groups of Benguet province, with the Ibaloi and Kalanguya.
Benguet's official provincial fruit is a native blueberry, known in Kankanaey as gotmo or alumani.

nations.name: Karen
nations.lands: Eastern Myanmar, including Karen State, and western and northern Thailand

facts.text: Karen is a name for several related peoples who speak 12 related Karenic languages; about 85 percent of Karen belong to the S'gaw or Pwo branches.
Karen communities have lived in what is now northern Thailand for many centuries.

nations.name: Kavalan
nations.lands: Yilan and the Hualien and Taitung coasts, Taiwan

facts.text: After a name rectification movement, the Kavalan were officially recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2002.
The Kavalan population was about 1,492 in January 2020.

nations.name: Khasi
nations.lands: Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, India, and nearby Bangladesh

facts.text: The Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council has a wing that oversees the Elakas, the traditional Khasi states.

source.title: General Administration Department and Elaka Administration

facts.text: Apart from Shillong's municipality and cantonment, all of Meghalaya is governed under the Sixth Schedule, the only northeast state where this is so.

nations.name: Kurukh
nations.lands: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal in India, with communities in Assam, Bangladesh and Nepal

facts.text: Odisha counted 358,112 Kurukh (Oraon) people in 2011; many farm and practice crafts such as carpentry, rope making and weaving date palm leaf mats.

source.title: Odisha State Tribal Museum: Oraon
source.publisher: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)

facts.text: Twelve to thirty Kurukh villages join in a Parha council, where members of each village council meet under a Parha chief.

source.title: Oraon
source.publisher: Dr. Ramdayal Munda Tribal Welfare Research Institute, Jharkhand

nations.name: Lumad
nations.lands: Mindanao, Philippines

facts.text: Lumad is a shared name for many Indigenous peoples of Mindanao, among them the Manobo, Subanon, Mandaya, Talandig and Teduray.
Lumad advocacy, with allies, helped write two important provisions into the 1987 Philippine Constitution.

nations.name: Magar
nations.lands: Hills of the Rapti and Gandaki river basins in western and central Nepal, and communities across Nepal

facts.text: Magar communities keep customary institutions such as the bheja, and each year they choose a mukhiya as community leader, who settles small disputes.

source.title: मगर (Magar)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Magar as an official language for both Gandaki and Karnali provinces.

source.title: Language Commission recommends province-wise official languages before government

nations.name: Marma
nations.lands: Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh

facts.text: Together, the Chakma, Marma and Tripura make up about 90 percent of the Indigenous peoples of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

nations.name: Mentawai
nations.lands: The Mentawai Islands, including Siberut, off West Sumatra, Indonesia

facts.text: On Siberut, a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1981, Mentawai communities use the forest with care, guided by traditional knowledge.

source.title: Siberut Biosphere Reserve, Indonesia
source.publisher: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme

facts.text: Siberut, home to many Mentawai communities, is the largest of the four Mentawai Islands west of Sumatra.

source.title: Siberut Biosphere Reserve, Indonesia
source.publisher: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme

nations.name: Mizo
nations.lands: Mizoram, northeast India

facts.text: Mizoram became a full state of India on 20 February 1987; its Legislative Assembly first met on 10 May 1972.
Historically, every Mizo village had its own chief, who was assisted by a council of elders.

nations.name: Mru
nations.lands: Bandarban district in the Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh, and nearby areas of Myanmar

facts.text: School textbooks up to class three have been published in the Mru language and alphabet.
The Mru alphabet, invented in the 1980s and unrelated to any other script, is encoded in the Unicode Standard with its own digits.

source.title: Chapter 13, South and Central Asia-II (The Unicode Standard, Version 18.0)

nations.name: Munda
nations.lands: Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Bihar in India, with communities in Bangladesh

facts.text: Mundari has its own script, known in the community as Mundari Bani; a version reformed in 2008 by Munda community bodies is in the Unicode Standard.

source.title: Chapter 13, South and Central Asia-II (The Unicode Standard, Version 18.0)

facts.text: The Munda call themselves Hodoko, which means human in their own language, Mundari.

source.title: Odisha State Tribal Museum: Munda
source.publisher: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)

nations.name: Naga
nations.lands: Nagaland, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh in India, and neighbouring Myanmar

facts.text: Nagaland's state portal lists 17 major tribes living in the state, each with its own language and festivals.

source.title: People and Culture
source.publisher: Nagaland State Portal, Government of Nagaland

facts.text: Each December the Government of Nagaland hosts the Hornbill Festival near Kohima, where all the state's tribes share their cultures.

nations.name: Newa
nations.lands: Swanigah, the Kathmandu Valley (Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur), and towns across Nepal

facts.text: Nepal Bhasa, the Newa language, has its own scripts, Ranjana and Prachalit, along with its own grammar, dictionaries and literature.

source.title: नेवार (Newar)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Nepal Bhasa, alongside Tamang, as an official language of Bagmati Province.

source.title: Language Commission recommends province-wise official languages before government

nations.name: Orang Asli
nations.lands: Peninsular Malaysia

facts.text: Orang Asli, a Malay collective term meaning original or first peoples, covers 18 officially listed groups of Peninsular Malaysia.
Some Temuan, Jakun and Semai families now run their own rubber, oil palm or cocoa farms.

nations.name: Paiwan
nations.lands: Southern Central Mountain Range across Pingtung and Taitung counties, Taiwan

facts.text: About 102,730 Paiwan people were counted in January 2020, living in the southern mountains of Pingtung and Taitung.
The Ravar branch of the Paiwan is known for outstanding carving and pottery.

nations.name: Pangcah
nations.lands: East of the Central Mountain Range in Hualien and Taitung counties, plus the Hengchun Peninsula, Taiwan

facts.text: Their own name, Pangcah, means people and kinsmen. The name Amis came from neighbours in Taitung and was later adopted by scholars.
In some Pangcah communities, each age class takes its name from a key event of its time, so one class name marks the computer era.

nations.name: Pinuyumayan
nations.lands: Taitung City and Beinan Township on the Taitung Plain, Taiwan

facts.text: Taitung City and Beinan Township on the Taitung Plain are the heart of Pinuyumayan life today.
About 14,517 Pinuyumayan people were counted in January 2020, and many have moved from eastern Taiwan to cities, where they are active in many fields.

nations.name: Rai
nations.lands: Majh Kirat, also called Khambuwan, in the middle hills of eastern Nepal between the Dudh Koshi and Arun rivers, plus Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari and the Kathmandu Valley

facts.text: The Kirat Rai Yayokkha, founded in 1990, works to unite Nepal's diverse Rai communities and to promote Rai languages, arts and literature.
The Rai are a multilingual people: the Kirat Rai Yayokkha has registered 26 Rai language groups, among them Bantawa, Chamling and Kulung.

source.title: राई (Rai)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

nations.name: Rukai
nations.lands: Southern Central Mountain Range in Kaohsiung, Pingtung and Taitung, Taiwan

facts.text: About 13,465 Rukai people were counted in January 2020, living in Kaohsiung, Pingtung and Taitung.
For the Rukai, the lily stands for purity and courage, and the right to wear lily ornaments sits at the heart of their culture.

nations.name: Saisiyat
nations.lands: Hsinchu and Miaoli counties in northwestern Taiwan

facts.text: The Saisiyat live in northwestern Taiwan, in Hsinchu County and Miaoli County on either side of Ngangihaw mountain.
The Saisiyat population was 6,730 in January 2020.

nations.name: Sakizaya
nations.lands: Hualien Plain, the East Rift Valley and coast, Taiwan

facts.text: Through a cultural revival led by the community itself, the Sakizaya were recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2007.
The Sakizaya population was about 985 in January 2020.

nations.name: Santal
nations.lands: Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and nearby states of India, northwest Bangladesh, and Nepal

facts.text: Santali, the Santal language, is one of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution.

source.title: Languages Included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
source.publisher: Department of Official Language, Ministry of Home Affairs, India

facts.text: On 25 December 2025, India's Constitution was released in the Santali language, written in the Ol Chiki script.

source.title: President of India releases the Constitution of India in the Santhali language

nations.name: Sediq
nations.lands: Mountain areas of Nantou and Hualien in central Taiwan

facts.text: Three subgroups make up the Sediq, each with its own group identity: Seediq Tgdaya, Sediq Toda and Sejiq Truku.
About 10,452 Sediq people were counted in January 2020, mostly in the mountains of Nantou and Hualien.

nations.name: Sherpa
nations.lands: Solukhumbu and the upper Dudh Koshi and Sun Koshi valleys of northeastern Nepal, from Solu to Helambu, and Kathmandu

facts.text: Sherpa communities use a customary system called nawa to look after crops and forests.

source.title: शेर्पा (Sherpa)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: In Nepal's 2021 census, 90.3 percent of Sherpa people reported Sherpa as their own language.

source.title: शेर्पा (Sherpa)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

nations.name: Tamang
nations.lands: Hills around the Kathmandu Valley and central Nepal

facts.text: The Tamang are on the Nepal government's official list of Adivasi Janajati, or Indigenous nationalities.

source.title: Adivasi Janajati list
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: Tamang is the mother tongue of about 4.88 percent of Nepal's population, according to the 2021 census.

nations.name: Tamu
nations.lands: Tamuwan, the hills between the Trishuli and Kali Gandaki rivers in central Nepal, including Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Syangja, Manang and Mustang

facts.text: Tamu Kyui, the Tamu language, now has its own Khema script, which Nepal's Language Commission has recognized.

source.title: गुरुङ(तमू) (Gurung, Tamu)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Gurung, the Tamu language, as an official language of Gandaki Province.

source.title: Language Commission recommends province-wise official languages before government

nations.name: Tao
nations.lands: Lanyu (Orchid Island), Taitung County, Taiwan

facts.text: The people call themselves Tao, meaning human, while Yami is the name used officially.
The Tao, who live on Lanyu, also called Orchid Island, numbered 4,684 in January 2020.

nations.name: Thao
nations.lands: Ita Thao Village by Sun Moon Lake and Dapinglin, Nantou County, Taiwan

facts.text: Thao people live mainly in Ita Thao Village in Yuchi Township and in Dapinglin, Shuili Township, both in Nantou County. They numbered about 817 in January 2020.
Thao oral history tells of ancestors who followed a white deer to Sun Moon Lake and found a fertile place full of fish.

nations.name: Tharu
nations.lands: The Terai plains of southern Nepal, and neighbouring India

facts.text: The Tharu are on the Nepal government's official list of Adivasi Janajati, or Indigenous nationalities.

source.title: Adivasi Janajati list
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: Tharu is the mother tongue of about 5.88 percent of Nepal's population, according to the 2021 census.

nations.name: Tripura
nations.lands: Chittagong Hill Tracts and other districts of Bangladesh, and the state of Tripura, India

facts.text: Tripura University opened a Department of Kokborok in 2015 and began doctoral research in the language in 2018.
Kokborok, the Tripura language, has been an official language of the Indian state of Tripura since 1979.

nations.name: Truku
nations.lands: Xiulin, Wanrong and Zhuoxi townships in Hualien County, Taiwan

facts.text: The Truku were officially recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2004.
About 32,333 Truku people were counted in January 2020, mostly in Hualien County.

nations.name: Tsou
nations.lands: Alishan Township in Chiayi County, plus Nantou and Kaohsiung, Taiwan

facts.text: The Tsou homeland centres on Alishan Township in Chiayi County, southwest of Yushan in central Taiwan.
The Tsou population was 6,702 in January 2020.

nations.name: Wanniyala-Aetto
nations.lands: Eastern Sri Lanka, including the Maduru Oya area

facts.text: In 1983, 51,468 hectares of Wanniyala-Aetto customary land were declared the Maduru Oya National Park.
Their own name, Wanniyala-Aetto, means forest dwellers, and their ancestors lived on the island long before the Sinhalese and the Tamils arrived.

nations.name: Yakthung
nations.lands: Limbuwan in the eastern hills of Nepal, including Taplejung, Panchthar, Terhathum and Ilam, plus Jhapa, Morang and Sunsari, with communities in Sikkim and Darjeeling, India

facts.text: In Nepal's 2021 census, 84.5 percent of Yakthung people reported Limbu as their mother tongue, a language with its own script, Sirijanga.

source.title: लिम्बु (Limbu)
source.publisher: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal

facts.text: Limbu, the Yakthung language, became an official language of Sikkim, India, in 1981, and its script is encoded in the Unicode Standard.

source.title: Chapter 13, South and Central Asia-II (The Unicode Standard, Version 18.0)

nations.name: Akwesasne
nations.lands: Along the St. Lawrence River where Ontario, Quebec and New York State meet, in Canada and the United States

facts.text: Akwesasne spans lands in Quebec, Ontario and New York State, and three separate but linked political bodies govern it.
Kanien'kéha, the Mohawk language, remains central to identity in Akwesasne and is actively taught in its schools.

nations.name: Anishinabek Nation
nations.lands: 39 First Nations across Ontario, Canada, from Pikwàkanagàn in the east and Aamjiwnaang in the south to Lake Nipigon in the north

facts.text: It is Ontario's oldest political organization, with roots in the Confederacy of Three Fires that long predates European contact.
The Anishinabek Nation speaks for 39 First Nations in Ontario with about 70,000 citizens, roughly one third of the province's First Nation population.

nations.name: Atikamekw
nations.lands: Nitaskinan in central Quebec, Canada, with the communities of Manawan, Wemotaci and Opitciwan

facts.text: The Atikamekw language, like other Algonquin and Anishinaabe languages, is rich in imagery and names things by how they truly are.
Young people aged 0 to 35 make up about 65 percent of the Atikamekw population today.

nations.name: Dene
nations.lands: Denendeh, the western Northwest Territories, Canada

facts.text: The Dene Nation brings together five regional groups, the Gwich'in, Sahtú, Deh Cho, Tłı̨chǫ and Akaitcho Dene, each with its own language and territory.
Dene simply means 'the people'. Their homeland, Denendeh, lies in the western Northwest Territories.

nations.name: Eeyou
also: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee)
nations.lands: Eeyou Istchee, the lands east of James Bay and Hudson Bay in northern Quebec, Canada

facts.text: Each Eeyou First Nation runs its own local government, and every elected Chief also sits on the board of the Grand Council of the Crees to address shared issues.

source.title: The Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee
source.publisher: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

facts.text: Eeyou Istchee is home to more than 20,000 people.

source.title: The Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee
source.publisher: Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee) / Cree Nation Government

nations.name: Gitxsan
nations.lands: The Laxyip along the upper Skeena River and its tributaries in northern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Gitxsan society is matriarchal, with four clans made up of independent Houses (Huwilp), each led by a Wii Simoogit, or high chief.
Gitxsanimaax, the traditional Gitxsan language, has two dialects: Giigeenix, spoken up river, and Gyeets, spoken down river.

nations.name: Haida Nation
nations.lands: Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the north coast of British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Council of the Haida Nation works to steward the lands and waters of Haida territories and carry Haida culture and language to future generations.
In April 2024 British Columbia and the Council of the Haida Nation signed the Rising Tide agreement, a first of its kind recognizing Haida Aboriginal title in Haida Gwaii.

source.title: For Immediate Release: Haida Nation, B.C. recognize Haida Aboriginal title, a historic first in Canada

nations.name: Haíɫzaqv
nations.lands: The Central Coast of British Columbia, Canada, centred on Bella Bella (Wáglísla) on Campbell Island

facts.text: In 2025 Heiltsuk members ratified a written constitution, a milestone in self-governance.
Haíɫzaqv means 'to speak and act correctly', principles that guide Heiltsuk ancestral and present-day ways of life.

nations.name: Innu
nations.lands: Nitassinan: Labrador (Newfoundland and Labrador) and eastern Quebec, Canada

facts.text: In 2008 the Innu Nation and Newfoundland and Labrador signed the Tshash Petapen, or New Dawn, Agreement.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

facts.text: The Innu Nation land claim, accepted for negotiation in 1978, covers about 70 percent of Labrador.

source.title: Innu Nation of Labrador
source.publisher: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Indigenous Affairs and Reconciliation

nations.name: Inuit
nations.lands: Inuit Nunangat: the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut, Nunavik and Nunatsiavut in Arctic Canada

facts.text: Roughly 60 percent of Inuit can hold a conversation in Inuktut, the Inuit language.
Most Inuit in Canada live in 51 communities across Inuit Nunangat, a homeland covering about 40 percent of Canada's land and 72 percent of its coastline.

nations.name: Inuit of Nunavut
nations.lands: Nunavut, Canada: the Qikiqtaaluk, Kivalliq and Kitikmeot regions

facts.text: Nunavut became Canada's newest territory on April 1, 1999, and Inuktitut is an official language of its government with Inuinnaqtun, English and French.
Signed on May 25, 1993, the Nunavut Agreement is the biggest Aboriginal land claims agreement ever made in Canada.

nations.name: Inuvialuit
nations.lands: The Inuvialuit Settlement Region in the western Arctic, Northwest Territories and Yukon, Canada

facts.text: Six communities lie within the Inuvialuit Settlement Region: Aklavik, Inuvik, Paulatuk, Sachs Harbour, Tuktoyaktuk and Ulukhaktok.
One of the agreement's basic goals is keeping Inuvialuit cultural identity and values strong as northern society changes.

nations.name: Kahnawà:ke
nations.lands: On the south shore of the St. Lawrence River, near Montreal, Quebec, Canada

facts.text: For more than a hundred years, many people from Kahnawà:ke, mostly men, have worked in the ironworking trade, much of it in the United States.
About 8,000 people live in Kahnawà:ke, on the banks of the St. Lawrence River about 10 kilometres south of Montreal.

nations.name: Kainai
nations.lands: Southern Alberta, Canada, with its main community at Standoff; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: The Blood Tribe's stated mission is to preserve and protect its lands, culture, language and traditions in the spirit of Kainayssini.
In 2026 the Blood Tribe Land Management Department won a Prairie Conservation Award.

nations.name: Ktunaxa
nations.lands: ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa: the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia, Canada, with Kootenay Tribes also based today in Montana and Idaho, United States

facts.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council helps represent the shared interests of four Ktunaxa First Nations within ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the Ktunaxa homelands.
ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the traditional territory, covers about 70,000 square kilometres in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia.

nations.name: Labrador Inuit
nations.lands: Nunatsiavut, on the north coast of Labrador, Canada

facts.text: The Nunatsiavut Government, the self-government of Labrador Inuit, officially came into being on December 1, 2005.
Nunatsiavut's legislative capital is Hopedale and its administrative capital is Nain.

nations.name: Mi’kmaq
nations.lands: Mi’kma’ki: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the Gaspé in Canada, with relatives in Maine, United States

facts.text: Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia wrote their own Netukulimk Livelihood Management Plans so members who fish can support themselves and their families.
In 2006 the 13 Mi'kmaw Chiefs of Nova Scotia formed the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs to guide the Nation's negotiators on rights and title.

nations.name: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation
nations.lands: Treaty 6 territory in central Saskatchewan, Canada, with urban reserve land in Saskatoon

facts.text: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation planned a gathering for August 20 to 23, 2026 to mark 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed.

source.title: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation, Band No. 102

facts.text: In 1988 Muskeg Lake Cree Nation created Asimakeniseekan Askiy in Saskatoon, the first commercial urban reserve in Canada.

nations.name: Nation Wendat
nations.lands: Wendake, near Québec City, within the traditional territory Onyionhwentsïio’ in Quebec, Canada

facts.text: After the Wendat language went dormant in the 1800s, the Yawenda project (2007 to 2012) brought language specialists and community members together to revive it.
The Nation counts more than 300 Wendat businesses, including many artisans, artists and cultural organizations.

nations.name: Nisg̱a’a Nation
nations.lands: The Nass River Valley (K’alii-Aksim-Lisims) in northwestern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nisg̱a’a, People of the Nass River, are a self-governing First Nation on Canada's Pacific Coast.
The Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement was the first modern treaty in British Columbia, and it recognizes both Nisg̱a’a Lands and the Nisg̱a’a Government.

nations.name: Nunavik Inuit
nations.lands: Nunavik, northern Quebec, Canada: 15 villages along Hudson Bay, Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay

facts.text: Makivvik, an Inuktitut name meaning 'to rise up', protects Nunavik Inuit rights under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, Canada's first comprehensive Inuit land claim.
Language retention among Nunavik Inuit is over 95 percent, and Inuktitut remains the main language spoken in the region.

nations.name: Nuu-chah-nulth
nations.lands: The west coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council serves fourteen Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations with about 10,000 members, grouped in three regions.
The Council's vision is self-government that builds strong, healthy Nuu-chah-nulth communities.

nations.name: Piikani Nation
nations.lands: Around Brocket in southern Alberta, Canada, near the Old Man River; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: Piikani stories, ceremonies and songs describe an ancestral territory reaching north to the North Saskatchewan River and west into the Rocky Mountains.
Piikani Nation had 3,928 registered members as of September 2026.

source.title: First Nation Profiles: Registered Population (Piikani Nation)
source.publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada

nations.name: Secwépemc
nations.lands: Secwepemcúl’ecw, a large territory in the interior of British Columbia, Canada, stretching from the Columbia River valley west to the Fraser River

facts.text: The Shuswap Nation Tribal Council brings together nine Secwépemc communities in the Southern Interior of British Columbia.
Secwépemc Chiefs formed the Shuswap Nation Tribal Council in 1980 to advance Aboriginal rights, self-government and the settlement of land title.

nations.name: Siksika Nation
nations.lands: East of Calgary, Alberta, Canada; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: Siksika's coat of arms, registered with the Canadian Heraldic Authority in June 1992, was the first registered by any Nation in Canada.
Siksika Nation has about 7,800 members, and its language is Siksika, or Blackfoot.

nations.name: Six Nations of the Grand River
nations.lands: Along the Grand River in southern Ontario, Canada

facts.text: It is the only First Nation community home to all six Haudenosaunee nations: Mohawk, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, Seneca and Tuscarora.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

facts.text: No First Nation in Canada has a larger population than Six Nations of the Grand River.

source.title: Who We Are
source.publisher: Six Nations of the Grand River

nations.name: Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw
nations.lands: The North Shore of Vancouver and the Squamish River valley, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nation's roots lie in several communities that became one government in 1923. Most members live on Vancouver's North Shore, others along the Squamish River.
The Squamish language is a sign of resilience: dozens of Nation members are learning it from their Elders as a second language.

nations.name: Syilx Okanagan Nation
nations.lands: The Okanagan, Similkameen and Nicola areas of British Columbia, Canada, and northern Washington State, United States

facts.text: Historically the Okanagan Nation Alliance represented eight member communities: seven in Canada and the Colville Confederated Tribes in Washington State.
The Okanagan Nation Alliance reports that the new Okanagan Dam Fish Passage, after years of advocacy and planning, lets salmon reach Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years.

nations.name: səlilwətaɬ
nations.lands: Burrard Inlet (səlilwət) in North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Tsleil-Waututh people see caring for the lands and waters of their territory as a birthright and obligation, so future generations can thrive.
Tsleil-Waututh means 'People of the Inlet'. The Nation's language is hən̓q̓əmin̓əm, in which its name is səlilwətaɬ.

nations.name: Tsuut’ina Nation
nations.lands: Treaty 7 territory in southern Alberta, Canada, bordering the city of Calgary

facts.text: Tsuut'ina Nation describes itself today as a highly sufficient and economically advanced First Nation.
Tsuut'ina is the only Dene-speaking nation in Treaty 7 territory, linked to the wider Dene Nation by its Athabaskan language.

nations.name: Tłı̨chǫ
nations.lands: Between Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories, Canada, around the communities of Behchokǫ̀, Whatì, Gamètì and Wekweètì

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Agreement, in effect since August 4, 2005, was the first combined land, resources and self-government agreement in the Northwest Territories.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

facts.text: The Tłı̨chǫ Government makes laws for its citizens in areas including education, child and family services, and Tłı̨chǫ language and culture.

source.title: Concluding and Implementing Land and Resources and Self-Government Agreements: Tłı̨chǫ
source.publisher: Government of the Northwest Territories, Executive and Indigenous Affairs

nations.name: Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation
nations.lands: Old Crow and the surrounding homeland in northern Yukon, Canada

facts.text: Old Crow, a fly-in community of about 300 people on the Porcupine River, is the seat of the Vuntut Gwitchin government.
Dinjii Zhuh k'yuu, the Gwich'in language, is the official language of the Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation, which is training teachers and raising young speakers.

nations.name: Wolastoqiyik
nations.lands: The Wolastoq (Saint John River) watershed, from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence: New Brunswick and Quebec in Canada, and Maine in the United States

facts.text: Six Wolastoqey communities in New Brunswick, Matawaskiye, Neqotkuk, Pilick, Sitansisk, Welamukotuk and Wotstak, work together through the Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick.
The Wolastoqiyik are the people of the Wolastoq watershed, a homeland of land, sea and fresh water reaching from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence River.

nations.name: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm
nations.lands: The Fraser River estuary, including much of Metro Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Musqueam is a strong, growing community of more than 1,300 members, many living on the Musqueam reserve near the mouth of the Fraser River.
The name xʷməθkʷəy̓əm means place of the məθkʷəy̓, a plant, and Musqueam people are traditionally hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ speakers.

nations.name: Akawaio
nations.lands: Upper Mazaruni area and nearby river valleys of western Guyana, with Akawaio also counted in Venezuela's census

facts.text: Kapohn is the Akawaio people's own name for themselves, and like most peoples of Guyana's interior they are Carib speakers.
Akawaio is one of the nine Indigenous languages covered by Guyana's language revival programme, which the government moved to restart in 2021.

source.title: Gov't to resume Amerindian language revival project
source.publisher: Department of Public Information, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Barí
nations.lands: Serranía de los Motilones and the Catatumbo and Oro river basins in Norte de Santander, Colombia, and Zulia state, Venezuela

facts.text: The Barí language, of the Chibcha family, is being passed on to new generations and has speakers of all ages.
Barí live in the foothills of Colombia's Serranía de los Motilones along the Catatumbo and Oro rivers, with settlements also in Zulia state, Venezuela.

nations.name: Parikwene
nations.lands: The Urukauá River in the Uaçá basin of Amapá, Brazil, and Saint-Georges-de-l'Oyapock, Cayenne and the lower Oyapock in French Guiana

facts.text: Parikwene families have villages in both Brazil and French Guiana and travel across the border often to visit kin and to trade.

source.title: Palikur
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: The Parikwene speak Parikwaki, a language of the Arawak family; their own name means 'the people of the river of the middle'.

source.title: Palikur
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Patamona
nations.lands: North and South Pakaraima Mountains and the Essequibo region of Guyana, including villages near Kaieteur Falls

facts.text: Like their Ingarikó relatives, the Patamona use Kapon as a self-designation in the border region shared by Guyana, Brazil and Venezuela.

source.title: Taurepang
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: Patamona communities live mainly in the North Pakaraima Mountains of Guyana, with others in the South Pakaraimas and the Essequibo region.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Pemón
nations.lands: Savannas of southeastern Venezuela, the Kamarang River area of Guyana, and Roraima state in Brazil

facts.text: Taurepang, Arekuna and Kamarakoto communities share the self-name Pemon, a word meaning 'people' or 'us'.

source.title: Taurepang
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In Guyana, Arekuna communities live on the banks of the Kamarang River.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Santa Rosa First Peoples Community
nations.lands: Arima, Trinidad, Trinidad and Tobago

facts.text: Trinidad and Tobago's government names the Santa Rosa First Peoples Community among the country's own Indigenous groups and holds a Day of Recognition every October 14.

source.title: Statement at the Special Permanent Council Meeting on the Commemoration of the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples 2018
source.publisher: Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs, Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago

facts.text: The community works to pass its culture on to younger generations and the wider public, serving as cultural ambassadors for Trinidad's First Peoples.

source.title: Celebrating Our First Peoples
source.publisher: National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago

nations.name: Taíno
nations.lands: Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and other islands of the Greater Antilles, and diaspora communities in the United States

facts.text: Over about four decades a Taíno movement has grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, as more families and groups affirm their Native ancestry.

source.title: Taino: Native Heritage and Identity in the Caribbean
source.publisher: Smithsonian Institution (National Museum of the American Indian and Smithsonian Latino Center)

facts.text: Taíno community groups take part in language research, including tracing the Taíno roots of everyday words such as hurricane, hammock and tobacco.

source.title: This Culture, Once Believed Extinct, Is Flourishing

nations.name: Tarëno
nations.lands: Southern Suriname along the Sipaliwini, Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers, and the Tumucumaque Indigenous Park in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: Suriname's association of Indigenous village leaders counts the Trio among the country's four large Indigenous peoples, living mainly in the south.

source.title: Dorpen en Dorpsbesturen
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

facts.text: In their own language the Tarëno say Wü Tarëno, 'I am Tarëno', meaning 'I am from here'; the names Trio and Tiriyó came from outsiders.

source.title: Tiriyó
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Teko
nations.lands: Camopi on the Oyapock River and Cayodé on the upper Maroni, French Guiana

facts.text: Teko and Wayãpi are the two Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in the Amazonian Park of French Guiana, where Wayana belongs to the Carib family.
France lists Teko, formerly called Émerillon, among French Guiana's six Amerindian languages recognized as languages of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

nations.name: Uwottüja
nations.lands: The Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers and the middle Orinoco, Amazonas state, Venezuela

facts.text: In 2020 Uwottüja communities of the Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers met at Pendare and declared themselves guardians of their territory.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

facts.text: The Uwottüja held their first congress as a people in 1984, uniting around the defense of their ancestral lands 'like one churuata, with one voice'.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

nations.name: Wai Wai
nations.lands: Kanashen in the far south of Guyana, and Indigenous lands in Pará, Amazonas and Roraima states, Brazil

facts.text: Waiwai, a Carib-family language, is the main language in Waiwai communities in Brazil, and most young people born there speak it.

source.title: Waiwai
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In 2007 the Wai Wai of Kanashen in southern Guyana made their titled forest a Community Owned Conservation Area; in 2017 it became a national protected area.

nations.name: Wajãpi
nations.lands: Wajãpi Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and the middle and upper Oyapock River in French Guiana

facts.text: In 1994 the Wajãpi began demarcating their own Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and founded the Council of Wajãpi Villages, known as Apina.

source.title: Wajãpi
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In French Guiana the Wayãpi live along the middle and upper Oyapock River.

nations.name: Warao
nations.lands: Orinoco Delta of Venezuela, the North West District of Guyana, and communities in Trinidad and Tobago

facts.text: Trinidad and Tobago's government names the Warao Nation of Trinidad and Tobago among the country's own Indigenous groups.

source.title: Statement at the Special Permanent Council Meeting on the Commemoration of the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples 2018
source.publisher: Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs, Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago

facts.text: In Guyana, where the name is spelled Warrau, Warao communities live in the wetlands of the North West District along the Barima and Pomeroon rivers.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Wayana
nations.lands: Upper Maroni River and its tributaries in French Guiana, the Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers in Suriname, and the East Paru River in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: Among younger people on Brazil's East Paru River, the Wayana language has gained great prestige.

source.title: Wayana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: France recognizes Wayana as one of six Amerindian languages of French Guiana with the status of a language of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

nations.name: Ye'kwana
nations.lands: Amazonas and Bolívar states in southern Venezuela, and the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers of Roraima, Brazil

facts.text: The name Ye'kwana, which the people use for themselves, entered Venezuela's census in 1982 and has almost fully replaced the outside name Makiritare.

source.title: Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda 2011: Empadronamiento de la Población Indígena

facts.text: Among themselves the Ye'kwana use So'to, meaning 'people', while Ye'kwana can be translated as 'canoe people'.

source.title: Ye'kwana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Yukpa
nations.lands: Sierra de Perijá on both sides of the border: Zulia state, Venezuela, and Cesar department, Colombia

facts.text: In Colombia, Yukpa resguardos are made up of settlements each led by a cabildo menor, with a cabildo mayor representing the people before the government.

source.title: Yukpa ywonku: Informe del estado de vitalidad de las lenguas nativas de Colombia

facts.text: Yukpa, a Carib-family language, has high vitality: in most communities speakers use it every day and make sure their children learn it.

source.title: Yukpa ywonku: Informe del estado de vitalidad de las lenguas nativas de Colombia

nations.name: Bribri
nations.lands: The Talamanca mountains of southern Costa Rica, on both the Caribbean (Limón) and Pacific (Puntarenas) sides, with smaller communities in Bocas del Toro, Panama

facts.text: The Bribri language is spoken on both sides of Costa Rica's Talamanca mountains, in Limón and Puntarenas, in three regional varieties named for Amubre, Coroma and Salitre.
Bribri communities also live in Panama, where the 2023 census counted 766 Bribri people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Buglé
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and nearby areas of Bocas del Toro and Veraguas in western Panama

facts.text: Under Panama's 1997 comarca law, the comarca's General Congress is the highest body for the ethnic and cultural voice and decisions of the Ngäbe-Buglé people.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 23,898 Buglé people; about 12,000 of them live in the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, which they share with the Ngäbe.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Cabécar
nations.lands: Indigenous territories in the Talamanca mountains and Chirripó area of Costa Rica, in Limón, Cartago and Puntarenas provinces

facts.text: Costa Rica's 2011 census found that 87.6 percent of people in the official Cabécar territories speak the Cabécar language.
Costa Rica's 2013 list of Indigenous territories includes Cabécar territories such as Alto Chirripó, Bajo Chirripó, Talamanca Cabécar, Ujarrás and Telire.

source.title: Anexo 6: Pueblos y territorios indígenas de Costa Rica (2013)

nations.name: Ch'orti'
nations.lands: Jocotán, Camotán, Olopa and Quezaltepeque in Chiquimula and La Unión in Zacapa, Guatemala, and communities around Copán in Honduras

facts.text: Ch'orti' is also spoken in Honduran communities such as Cabañas, Santa Rita and Copán Ruinas.

source.title: Descubre los útiles escolares en idioma ch'orti'

facts.text: In 2025 the Academy of Mayan Languages of Guatemala translated the national symbols into Ch'orti'; the flag, for example, is tz'apray b'ujk.

source.title: Símbolos patrios en ch'orti: un aporte para preservar el idioma y la identidad

nations.name: Emberá
nations.lands: The Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands in Darién and eastern Panama, and the Pacific and Chocó regions of Colombia

facts.text: Panama's Law 22 of 1983 created the Emberá comarca in Darién and named its General Congress the highest traditional decision-making body of the Emberá people.

source.title: Ley 22 de 1983, por la cual se crea la Comarca Emberá de Darién
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Bilingual storybooks in Emberá and Spanish are among the learning materials made for the early education of Emberá children in Panama.

source.title: La educación intercultural bilingüe en Panamá
source.publisher: UNICEF Latin America and the Caribbean

nations.name: Garifuna
nations.lands: Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, plus large diaspora communities

facts.text: In 2024, Belize observed Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November as one of its official public holidays.
Most Garifuna communities today are in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, and the Garifuna language is part of the Arawakan family.

source.title: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna

nations.name: Guna
nations.lands: Gunayala on Panama's Caribbean coast and islands, plus Madungandí and Wargandí in Panama and communities in northwestern Colombia

facts.text: Gunayala's 49 communities govern themselves together through the Guna General Congress, their highest political and administrative body for land, resources and education.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

facts.text: Gunayala runs along Panama's Caribbean coast to the Colombian border, with about 315 km of coastline and over 400 small islands and islets.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

nations.name: Ixil
nations.lands: The Ixil region of northern Quiché, Guatemala: Nebaj, Chajul and Cotzal

facts.text: Ixil women weavers of the Q'imb'al initiative, with youth and village ancestral authorities, launched Community Radio Tiichajil Tenam in Nebaj to share Ixil cultural values.

source.title: Radio Tiichajil Tenam Becomes a Reality

facts.text: In 2020 Guatemala's Constitutional Court ruled in favor of the Maya Ixil people of Nebaj, restoring their ownership of the communal land of Ak'ul.

source.title: Pueblos Mayas Ixiles y Ch'orti's recuperan certeza jurídica sobre sus tierras

nations.name: K'iche'
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala, including Quiché, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango and Sololá

facts.text: In Totonicapán, the 48 Cantones is a K'iche' ancestral authority built from community governments, with representatives chosen each year in assembly.

source.title: Former Indigenous authorities of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán released in Guatemala after more than a year in pretrial detention

facts.text: The 48 Cantones' system of caring for forests and water has served as an example for communities all over Guatemala.

nations.name: Kaliña
nations.lands: Coastal Suriname and French Guiana, with related communities in Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil

facts.text: In Suriname the Kari'na (Kaliña) live in many villages with their own village heads, including Christiaankondre and Langamankondre at Galibi in Marowijne district.

source.title: Dorpen en Dorpsbesturen
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

facts.text: Suriname's Indigenous village leaders say legal recognition of collective rights is an obligation, not a policy choice, and in 2026 urged full implementation of the Kaliña and Lokono judgment.

source.title: VIDS dient resolutie in: Voer Kaliña & Lokono-vonnis uit
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

nations.name: Kalinago
nations.lands: The Kalinago Territory on the northeast coast of Dominica, in the eastern Caribbean

facts.text: In July 2024, voters in the Kalinago Territory elected their Kalinago Chief; the winning candidate received about 58 percent of the votes counted.
The Kalinago Territory has its own local government: a Chief and six councillors elected by residents every five years, alongside representation in Dominica's parliament.

source.title: The Kalinago Territory
source.publisher: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

nations.name: Kaqchikel
nations.lands: Central highlands of Guatemala, including Chimaltenango, Sacatepéquez and parts of Sololá

facts.text: Community Radio Naköj in Santo Domingo Xenacoj, working since 2013, produces programs in Kaqchikel and Spanish for about 7,000 Kaqchikel listeners.

source.title: 2020 Community Media COVID-19 Emergency Grant Partners

facts.text: In 2021 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled in favor of the Maya Kaqchikel of Sumpango and other communities, upholding Indigenous rights to free expression through community radio.

source.title: Historic Win: Inter-American Court of Human Rights Rules in Favor of Indigenous Peoples

nations.name: Lenca
nations.lands: Western and southwestern Honduras (Intibucá, Lempira, La Paz and nearby departments) and eastern El Salvador

facts.text: COPINH runs Lenca community radio stations that share news bulletins, podcasts, interviews and training with Lenca communities.

source.title: Las palabras haciendo eco en los caminos del pueblo Lenca: COPINH

facts.text: A community journalism program trained 24 Lenca women and 17 men as community correspondents, starting during the COVID-19 pandemic.

source.title: Indigenous, Garifuna, and Feminist Community Correspondents Push for a More Inclusive Democracy

nations.name: Lokono
nations.lands: Coastal and river villages of Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana

facts.text: Suriname's association of Indigenous village leaders lists the Lokono among the country's four major Indigenous peoples, with villages such as Washabo, Apoera and Alfonsdorp.

source.title: Dorpen en Dorpsbesturen
source.publisher: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)

facts.text: Lokono village representatives founded Wadian Bokotothi, meaning 'Language Keepers', and helped share one common Lokono spelling across Suriname, French Guiana and Guyana.

source.title: State-of-the-Art in the Development of the Lokono Language
source.publisher: Language Documentation & Conservation, University of Hawai'i Press

nations.name: Mam
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala (Huehuetenango, San Marcos, Quetzaltenango) and neighboring Chiapas, Mexico

facts.text: In October 2025, the Mam communities of Cajolá and Todos Santos Cuchumatán joined two other Maya communities in reporting to a UN committee on their community radio rights.

source.title: Indigenous Communities and Cultural Survival Urge CERD to Address Community Radio Rights Violations in Guatemala

facts.text: B'alam Stereo in Cabricán, among the longer-running Indigenous stations in Guatemala's highlands, has served the Maya Mam since 1976, with work promoting education, health, water and justice.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

nations.name: Mayangna
nations.lands: The Bosawás region and North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua, with related Tawahka communities in Honduras

facts.text: After the 2020 hurricanes, Mayangna communities in Bonanza rebuilt together: they repaired 15 roofs collectively and planted 50 plots of grains, beans, corn and cassava.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

facts.text: Nicaragua's Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, in the Mosquitia region, is ancestral territory of the Mayangna and Miskitu peoples, whose rights there are recognized.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

nations.name: Miskitu
nations.lands: The Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and La Moskitia in northeastern Honduras, along the Wangki (Coco) River

facts.text: In 2021 the Yapti Tasba community radio network, linked to Miskitu organization YATAMA, reached 17 Indigenous territories and 154 communities, 95 percent of them Miskitu.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

facts.text: Nicaragua's Caribbean Coast autonomy law affirms that Indigenous communities there have the right to keep and develop their languages and to bilingual education.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

nations.name: Mopan
nations.lands: The Toledo District of southern Belize and nearby Petén, Guatemala

facts.text: In 2022 a Free, Prior and Informed Consultation Protocol for the Maya of southern Belize was adopted, and in 2025 a working draft on protecting Maya customary land tenure followed.

source.title: Closing Remarks at the Final Monitoring Hearing in Maya Leaders v The Attorney General of Belize [2015] CCJ 15 (AJ)

facts.text: A 2015 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment obliges Belize's government to mark out and register Maya village lands in the south and guard them against outsiders.

source.title: Maya Q'eqchi and Mopan of Southern Belize Win Major Land Rights Victory in International Appeals Court (statement by the Maya Leaders Alliance)

nations.name: Nahuat Pipil
nations.lands: Western El Salvador, especially Sonsonate and Ahuachapán departments

facts.text: Izalco is the only municipality in El Salvador with an ancestral Indigenous government, made up of mayordomos and mayordomas.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

facts.text: In Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Nahuat-speaking teachers created Nahuatl cribs where children learn the language, and Radio Sensunat promotes Nahuat Pipil culture.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

nations.name: Naso Tjër Di
nations.lands: The Naso Tjër Di comarca along the Teribe River in Bocas del Toro, northwestern Panama, near the Costa Rican border

facts.text: The Naso are led by a king who lives in Sieyik, where Panama's president came in 2020 to sign the law creating their comarca.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

facts.text: In December 2020 Panama created the 1,600 square kilometer Naso Tjër Di comarca, the result of decades of Naso efforts to secure their land rights.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

nations.name: Ngäbe
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca in western Panama (parts of Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí and Veraguas), nearby lands in Panama, and Ngäbe territories in southern Costa Rica

facts.text: Panama's Law 10 of 1997 created the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and made its lands the collective property of the comarca, closed to private sale.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 444,878 Ngäbe people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Q'eqchi'
nations.lands: Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Petén in Guatemala, and the Toledo District of southern Belize

facts.text: Radio Chiquixji in Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, broadcasts for bilingual Q'eqchi' and Spanish speakers and for communities that speak only Q'eqchi'.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: In southern Belize, 39 Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya communities have rights to their customary lands, as Belize's highest appeals court affirmed in 2015.

source.title: Maya Leaders Alliance Advocates at United Nations Urging Respect for Rule of Law in Belize

nations.name: Tz'utujil
nations.lands: The southern shore of Lake Atitlán in Sololá, Guatemala, including Santiago Atitlán and San Pedro La Laguna

facts.text: In Santiago Atitlán, a Tz'utujil traditional authority welcomed Indigenous youth from three countries in 2013 and spoke in Tz'utujil about the role of ancestral authorities.

source.title: Indigenous Mayan Youth Forge International Relationships Based on Community Radio

facts.text: Radio Sembrador, a community station in San Pedro La Laguna on Lake Atitlán, broadcasts news and cultural programs in Tz'utujil and Spanish.

source.title: Profile of A Community Radio Station: Radio Sembrador

nations.name: Wayuu
nations.lands: The Guajira Peninsula, shared by northern Colombia (La Guajira) and northwestern Venezuela (Zulia)

facts.text: Wayuu justice rests on dialogue: respected mediators called Pütchipü'üi, or palabreros, settle disputes between clans through repair and compensation. UNESCO listed this system in 2010.

source.title: Wayuu normative system, applied by the Pütchipü'üi (palabrero)

facts.text: The Wayuu live on the Guajira Peninsula, which spans the border between Colombia and Venezuela.

source.title: Wayuu normative system, applied by the Pütchipü'üi (palabrero)

nations.name: Wounaan
nations.lands: Darién and eastern Panama, including the Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands, and the San Juan River region of Colombia

facts.text: Wounaan forest technicians map illegal clearing with smartphone apps and GIS, and communities bring that evidence to the Wounaan National Congress.

source.title: Panama's Indigenous Groups Wage High-Tech Fight for Their Lands
source.publisher: Yale Environment 360, Yale School of the Environment

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 10,634 Wounaan people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Xinka
nations.lands: Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Jalapa departments in southeastern Guatemala

facts.text: In May 2024 the Parliament of the Xinka People hosted Guatemala's president in San Juan de Arana, Cuilapa, where they signed a 13-point work agenda.

source.title: Alegres le abrimos las puertas de nuestra casa, como usted nos ha abierto las puertas del Palacio, dice el pueblo xinca al presidente Arévalo

facts.text: In Santa Rosa, the Xinka People's Council (COPXIG), a local cooperative and the departmental education office work together to restore and teach the Xinka language.

source.title: Historia e Identidad del Pueblo Xinka
source.publisher: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Dirección General de Investigación

nations.name: Ayuuk
nations.lands: The Sierra Mixe of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Tlahuitoltepec, Tamazulapam, Ayutla and Guichicovi

facts.text: Backstrap loom weaving continues in Tamazulapam, Tlahuitoltepec and Cotzocón, and young Ayuuk artists are taking up mural and canvas painting.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: In the Ayuuk language the word for a festival is xëëw, which also means day, sun, time and name.

source.title: Mixes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Binnizá
nations.lands: The Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico, including Juchitán and Tehuantepec

facts.text: Velas, festivals honoring patron saints, family names, trades and places, are a central Binnizá institution; Juchitán alone celebrates about 24 of them.

source.title: Zapotecos (del Istmo, Valles centrales y Sierra Norte) : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ch'ol
nations.lands: Northern Chiapas, Mexico, including Tila, Tumbalá, Palenque, Sabanilla and Salto de Agua

facts.text: La Voz de la Selva, a Chiapas public radio station on air since 2000 in Santo Domingo, Ocosingo, broadcasts in Spanish, Tseltal, Ch'ol and Lacandón.

source.title: XHSDM-FM La Voz de la Selva : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Maize is at the heart of Ch'ol culture, and many festivals follow the farming year, from preparing the fields and sowing to the harvest.

source.title: Ch'oles : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Dibaku
nations.lands: La Cañada region of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Cuicatlán, Concepción Pápalo and Santos Reyes Pápalo

facts.text: Since 1991, La Voz de la Chinantla has broadcast with bilingual staff in Chinantec, Mazatec and Cuicatec, recording music and oral tradition with communities.

source.title: XEOJN La Voz de la Chinantla (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: The Cuicatec region lies in northeastern Oaxaca, in the area known as La Cañada, covering about 8,400 square kilometers across ten municipalities.

source.title: Cuicatecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ha shuta enima
nations.lands: The Sierra Mazateca of northern Oaxaca around Huautla de Jiménez, Mexico, and nearby parts of Veracruz

facts.text: The sound archive of La Voz de la Chinantla, an INPI station in Oaxaca, holds over 5,000 music recordings, including Mazatec huehuentones musicians.

source.title: XEOJN La Voz de la Chinantla (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Mazatecs call themselves Ha shuta enima, which in their language means those who work the hills, humble people of custom.

source.title: Mazatecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura

nations.lands: The lagoons and coast of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico: San Mateo del Mar, San Dionisio del Mar and San Francisco del Mar

source.title: Huaves : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México
