nations.name: A:shiwi
nations.lands: Pueblo of Zuni along the Zuni River in western New Mexico, US, with reservation land in Arizona

facts.text: The Pueblo of Zuni counts about 18,692 people and holds about 463,287 acres of reservation land.
For about the last 300 years most Zuni people have lived in one main village, the Pueblo of Zuni, with farming villages used at planting and harvest.

nations.name: Acoma
nations.lands: Acoma Mesa and surrounding lands in west-central New Mexico, US

facts.text: Since 2017 the Acoma Language Program has been building a Keres dictionary, with about 5,000 words and phrases being edited by fluent speakers.
In 1999 Acoma set up a Historic Preservation Office to keep traditional skills alive, among them stone cutting, wood carving, pottery making and weaving.

nations.name: Akimel O’otham
nations.lands: Gila River Indian Community, south of Phoenix, Arizona, US, shared with the Pee Posh (Maricopa)

facts.text: The Akimel O’otham welcomed the Pee Posh (Maricopa) to the Gila River long ago, and the two peoples still share its lands and resources today.
Akimel O’otham basket weaving is in revival, and in 2004 the community dedicated the Huhugam Heritage Center to care for its heritage.

nations.name: Cocopah
nations.lands: Lower Colorado River and delta: south of Yuma and near Somerton, Arizona, US, and the Mexicali valley of Baja California and San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: About 1,000 Cocopah tribal members live and work on or near their reservation south of Yuma, Arizona, which was established in 1917.
Since 2003 the Cucapá of El Mayor, Baja California, and the Cocopah of Somerton, Arizona, have met each year with dances, songs, crafts and food.

source.title: Cucapás
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Comcaac
nations.lands: Desert coast of Sonora on the Gulf of California, Mexico, including Punta Chueca, El Desemboque and Tiburón Island

facts.text: In 1975 Mexico declared the Canal del Infiernillo an exclusive Comcaac fishing zone and symbolically granted them Tiburón Island, a nature reserve, as communal land.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Comcaac artisans weave coritas, baskets made since before Spanish contact. A very large one can take a year or two to finish.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Diné
nations.lands: Diné Bikéyah (Navajoland) across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, US

facts.text: The Navajo Nation Council, the Nation’s governing body, has 24 delegates elected from legislative districts.
Diné Bikéyah, the Navajo Nation, covers more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, larger than 10 of the 50 US states.

nations.name: Havasu Baaja
nations.lands: Havasu Canyon in the Grand Canyon, Arizona, US (village of Supai)

facts.text: Supai is so remote that the US Postal Service carries all mail in and out of the canyon by mule train.
The Havasupai reservation was set up in 1880 and greatly enlarged in 1975. It covers 188,077 acres beside the South Rim of the Grand Canyon.

nations.name: Hopi
nations.lands: Hopitutskwa, northeastern Arizona, US (Navajo and Coconino counties)

facts.text: Hopi government is unicameral. Its powers rest with a Tribal Council of village representatives, who serve two year terms.
The Hopi Reservation in northeastern Arizona covers more than 1.5 million acres and is made up of 12 villages on three mesas.

source.title: The Official Website of the Hopi Tribe

nations.name: Hualapai
nations.lands: Northwestern Arizona, US, along the Grand Canyon and Colorado River (Peach Springs)

facts.text: The name Hualapai means People of the Tall Pines.
The Hualapai Reservation, set up in 1883, covers about one million acres along 108 miles of the Grand Canyon and Colorado River.

nations.name: Jicarilla Apache
nations.lands: North-central New Mexico, US, along the Colorado line and across the Continental Divide (Dulce)

facts.text: The Jicarilla Apache Nation reservation spans more than 879,917 acres in north-central New Mexico, and Dulce is its only community and tribal headquarters.
After 1887 the Jicarilla moved their individual allotments back into tribal ownership, keeping their lands and water rights together.

nations.name: Kha’P’o
nations.lands: From the eastern Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: People of Santa Clara Pueblo still speak the Tewa language today and carry on their customs and cultural activities.
Santa Clara is one of six Tewa-speaking villages, and its reservation covers about 90 square miles from the Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande.

nations.name: Kumeyaay
nations.lands: San Diego and Imperial counties, California, US, and Tecate, Ensenada and Rosarito in Baja California, Mexico

facts.text: North of the US and Mexico border there are 12 Kumeyaay Nation bands today, each original to Kumeyaay territory. Sycuan is one of them.

source.title: History & Heritage
source.publisher: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation

facts.text: In Baja California the Kumiai call themselves Tipai. Their communities sit on the coastal plateaus of Ensenada and Rosarito and in Tecate.

source.title: Kumiais
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Mescalero Apache
nations.lands: South-central New Mexico, US (Mescalero Apache Reservation)

facts.text: Today three peoples, the Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua Apache, together make up the Mescalero Apache Tribe on a 463,000 acre reservation.
The Mescalero Apache Tribe owns and runs the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and the Ski Apache ski area.

source.title: Official Website of the Mescalero Apache Tribe

nations.name: Nuche
also: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
nations.lands: Southwestern Colorado (Ignacio, Towaoc), northeastern Utah (Uintah and Ouray) and nearby New Mexico and Utah lands, US

facts.text: There are three Ute tribes today: the Southern Ute (Mouache and Capote bands), the Ute Mountain Ute (Weenuche band) and the Northern Ute in Utah.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe teaches the Ute language to Head Start children ages 2 to 5 and holds evening language classes for adults.

nations.name: Ohkay Owingeh
nations.lands: Where the Rio Grande and Rio Chama meet, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Ohkay Owingeh is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.
The people have long called their home Ohkay Owingeh, place of the strong people in Tewa, and officially restored that name in place of San Juan, given in 1598.

nations.name: Rarámuri
nations.lands: Sierra Tarahumara in Chihuahua, Mexico, with smaller communities in Durango, Sonora and Sinaloa

facts.text: The Rarámuri ball race is a contest in which runners cover long distances while kicking a wooden ball, and it is held as part of community fiestas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Rarámuri artisans make violins, drums, palm baskets, clay pots and wooden masks, and sell them in towns such as Guachochi, Creel and Batopilas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: San Carlos Apache
nations.lands: Gila, Graham and Pinal counties, southeastern Arizona, US

facts.text: The San Carlos Apache Reservation, set aside in 1871, covers 1,834,781 acres reaching from alpine meadows to desert in southeastern Arizona.
More than a third of San Carlos land is forest or woodland, giving a home to elk, mule deer, black bear, turkeys and mountain lion.

nations.name: Southern Paiute
nations.lands: Southern Utah and northern Arizona, US, including Cedar City, Utah, and the Kaibab reservation near Fredonia, Arizona

facts.text: The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Restoration Act of April 3, 1980 brought formal federal recognition to the Cedar Band of Paiute Indians.
The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah shares The Paiute Language for Beginners, now in its second edition, which anyone can view and download.

nations.name: Taos Pueblo
nations.lands: Taos valley, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Tiwa is the native language of Taos Pueblo, and English and Spanish are also spoken there.
In 1970 a federal law returned 48,000 acres, including Blue Lake, to Taos Pueblo, a landmark for tribal self-determination across the United States.

nations.name: Tohono O’odham
nations.lands: Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona, US (Sells is the capital), with O’odham communities across the border in Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: Divided by the border since the 1850s, O’odham communities in Sonora, Mexico, and Arizona still share a common culture and sense of being one people.

source.title: Pápagos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: O’odham groups still speak the O’odham language, part of the Uto-Aztecan family, with dialects that vary from group to group.

nations.name: Warihó and Macurawe
nations.lands: Foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental on the Chihuahua and Sonora border, Mexico

facts.text: The people call themselves Macurawe in Sonora and Warihó in Chihuahua. Their Uto-Aztecan language has two variants and bridges Tarahumara and Mayo.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Warihó and Macurawe families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. Their craft work is family based and rests with women.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: White Mountain Apache
nations.lands: White Mountains of east-central Arizona, US (Fort Apache Indian Reservation, Whiteriver)

facts.text: The White Mountain Apache own and run Sunrise, one of the largest ski resorts in the Southwest, and rare Apache trout swim in reservation streams.
White Mountain Apache people live on 1.6 million acres of their ancestral homeland, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, set aside in 1891.

nations.name: Wixárika
nations.lands: Sierra Madre Occidental in Jalisco and Nayarit, Mexico, with communities in Durango and Zacatecas

facts.text: At the end of the 1700s Wixárika communities received land titles that defined the boundaries of their present-day communities.

source.title: Huicholes
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: In July 2025 UNESCO added the Wixárika Route through sacred sites to Wirikuta, a 500 km corridor, to the World Heritage List after decades of Wixaritari requests.

source.title: Boletín No. 334: La Ruta Wixárika por los sitios sagrados a Wirikuta es inscrita en la Lista de Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH)

nations.name: Yavapai
nations.lands: Central and western Arizona, US, including Fort McDowell near Phoenix and Prescott

facts.text: In September 2026 the Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation, about 950 members, marked 123 years since its land was set aside in 1903.

source.title: Welcome to Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation

facts.text: In 1976 Fort McDowell Yavapai community members voted 144 to 57 against selling their land for the Orme Dam, and in 1981 the dam was called off.

nations.name: Yoeme
nations.lands: Yaqui River valley in Sonora, Mexico, and Pascua Yaqui communities near Tucson, Arizona, US

facts.text: Most Yoeme people today live in the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa, and the federally recognized Pascua Yaqui Tribe is based in Tucson, Arizona.
The Pascua Yaqui Tribe in Arizona gained United States federal recognition on September 18, 1978.

nations.name: Yoreme
nations.lands: Southern Sonora (Etchojoa, Huatabampo, Navojoa) and northern Sinaloa (Ahome, El Fuerte, Guasave), Mexico

facts.text: Yoreme communities have traditional governors. In December 2025 they met Mexico’s federal agrarian office to set a path for continuing the Yoreme-Mayo Justice Plan.

source.title: Atienden Plan de Justicia al pueblo Yoreme-Mayo de Sonora

facts.text: Yoreme patron saint fiestas strengthen the social networks that link communities across Mayo lands and keep Yoreme identity alive.

source.title: Mayos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Aṉangu
nations.lands: Central Australia, including Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa in the Northern Territory and the APY Lands of South Australia

facts.text: The park's board of management has 12 people, including eight Aboriginal members nominated by Traditional Owners.

source.title: Joint management | Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park | Parks Australia

facts.text: Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park was handed back to its Aṉangu Traditional Owners in 1985 and is jointly managed today.

source.title: Joint management | Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park | Parks Australia

nations.name: Arrernte
nations.lands: Alice Springs and surrounding lands in Central Australia, Northern Territory, Australia

facts.text: Lhere Artepe Aboriginal Corporation, their native title body, looks after five Indigenous Land Use Agreements plus a land release agreement.

source.title: About Us | Lhere Artepe Aboriginal Corporation

facts.text: Arrernte people from three estate groups, Antulye, Irlpme and Mparntwe, are the traditional owners of Alice Springs and its surrounding land.

source.title: About Us | Lhere Artepe Aboriginal Corporation

nations.name: Chuukese
nations.lands: Chuuk State in the Federated States of Micronesia, on the high islands of Chuuk Lagoon such as Weno, Tonoas, Uman and Fefan, and outlying atolls

facts.text: Chuuk's state constitution says existing Chuukese custom and tradition shall be respected, and lets traditional leaders hold formal roles in government.

source.title: Chuuk State Constitution, Article IV
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

facts.text: Chuuk's constitution recognizes traditional rights over all reefs, tidelands and other submerged lands, including the water above them.

source.title: Chuuk State Constitution, Article IV
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

nations.name: Cook Islands Māori
nations.lands: the Cook Islands, including Rarotonga and the Southern and Northern Group islands

facts.text: Te Maeva Nui, held every early August, marks Cook Islands self-governance on 4 August and gathers communities from every island for song, dance, drumming and chant.
A 2003 law declared Cook Islands Māori an official language of the Cook Islands, alongside English, and set up a Māori language commission.

source.title: Te Reo Maori Act 2003 (Cook Islands)
source.publisher: Université Laval, CEFAN: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde

nations.name: Gadigal
nations.lands: The southern side of Sydney Harbour (Port Jackson), from South Head to around Petersham, in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia

facts.text: Descendants of the Eora still live in Sydney today and proudly use the name Eora.
The City of Sydney formally acknowledges the Gadigal of the Eora Nation as the traditional custodians of the place now called Sydney.

nations.name: Gamilaraay
nations.lands: North-central New South Wales into southern Queensland, Australia

facts.text: The Australian National University teaches Gamilaraay as a heritage language that its custodians are actively reviving.

source.title: Gamilaraay - Introduction to an Australian Indigenous Language

facts.text: Student work in the ANU Gamilaraay course feeds into materials for Gamilaraay and Yuwaalaraay language revival, taught with a free textbook called Wiidhaa.

source.title: Gamilaraay - Introduction to an Australian Indigenous Language

nations.name: Gunantuna
nations.lands: the Gazelle Peninsula of New Britain Island, East New Britain Province, Papua New Guinea

facts.text: Diwarra pays for everyday things such as store goods and school fees, and sharing it out expresses ties between clans and individuals.

source.title: Gunantuna (Tolai people)
source.publisher: Queensland Art Gallery | Gallery of Modern Art

facts.text: In 2016 a Queensland gallery commissioned A Bit na Ta, a collaborative work made with the wider Tolai community whose music carries the rhythms of Tolai life from 1875 to 1975.

source.title: Art from Papua New Guinea Celebrated in Major QAG Exhibition
source.publisher: Queensland Art Gallery | Gallery of Modern Art

nations.name: Gunditjmara
nations.lands: South-west Victoria, including Budj Bim and Tae Rak (Lake Condah), Australia

facts.text: Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation was set up in 2005 to continue Gunditjmara connection to country, including native title work.

source.title: Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation | GMTOAC | 248 Condah Estate Road, Heywood VIC, Australia
source.publisher: Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation

facts.text: All of the Budj Bim Cultural Landscape is Aboriginal owned or managed.

source.title: World heritage conservation of Budj Bim

nations.name: I-Kiribati
nations.lands: the Republic of Kiribati in the central Pacific, across the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands

facts.text: In Kiribati the mwaneaba, the traditional meeting house, is where village decisions are made by the unimwane, the senior men, whose seating shows their standing.

source.title: Te Mwaneaba ni Kiribati: The Traditional Meeting House of Kiribati
source.publisher: Shima: The International Journal of Research into Island Cultures

facts.text: In 2010 the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, about 408,250 square kilometres of ocean and islands, became the first World Heritage site in Kiribati.

nations.name: iTaukei
nations.lands: Fiji

facts.text: The iTaukei Land Trust Board, set up in 1940, manages iTaukei land for its owners, whether a yavusa, mataqali or tokatoka.
The iTaukei Affairs Board, set up in 1944 as the Fijian Affairs Board, is the main advisory and coordinating body for iTaukei affairs, supporting village, tikina and provincial leaders.

nations.name: Kanak
nations.lands: New Caledonia, including Grande Terre and the Loyalty Islands

facts.text: Since 2016 every pupil in New Caledonia must be taught the fundamentals of Kanak culture, and every school must offer teaching in Kanak languages.

source.title: Organisation coutumière kanak
source.publisher: Institut de la statistique et des études économiques Nouvelle-Calédonie (ISEE)

facts.text: Kanak society is organised by custom: clans join into tribes within customary districts, which are grouped into eight customary areas.

source.title: Organisation coutumière kanak
source.publisher: Institut de la statistique et des études économiques Nouvelle-Calédonie (ISEE)

nations.name: Kaurna
nations.lands: The Adelaide Plains of South Australia, from around Crystal Brook in the north, bounded by the Mount Lofty Ranges to the east, Australia

facts.text: In March 2018 Kaurna people were recognised as native title holders around Adelaide, the first positive native title determination over a capital city area.

source.title: Native Title Recognition For Kaurna People Over Adelaide Area

facts.text: Requests for Kaurna names and translations all go through Kaurna Warra Karrpanthi, an Aboriginal corporation.

source.title: Aboriginal people of South Australia: Kaurna

nations.name: Kosraeans
nations.lands: Kosrae, an island state in the east of the Federated States of Micronesia, with the municipalities of Lelu, Malem, Tafunsak and Utwe

facts.text: Kosrae State has its own constitutional government, with a legislature elected by voters in the districts of Lelu, Malem, Tafunsak and Utwe.

source.title: Kosrae
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

facts.text: In 2017 Kosraean elders proposed protecting Kosrae's mountain range, seen as the figure Mahkontowe, now the Mahkontowe Conservation Area under Kosrae State law.

nations.name: Larrakia
nations.lands: The Darwin region, from Cox Peninsula in the west to Gunn Point in the north, Northern Territory, Australia

facts.text: Larrakia Nation Aboriginal Corporation, set up in 1997, runs about 40 programs in Darwin, including the Larrakia Land and Sea Rangers.
Larrakia are the traditional owners of the Darwin region, with country reaching from Cox Peninsula in the west up to Gunn Point in the north.

nations.name: Mā'ohi
nations.lands: French Polynesia, including Tahiti and the other islands of its five archipelagos

facts.text: A new website interface announced in 2017 by the Tahitian Academy, Fare Vāna'a, adds French to Tahitian search to its Tahitian to French dictionary.

source.title: Evolution du site internet du Fare Vāna’a & application
source.publisher: Service public de la Polynésie française (DGEN)

facts.text: UNESCO honours mā'ohi skill in sailing outrigger canoes across long stretches of ocean, navigating by observing natural phenomena.

nations.name: Marshallese
nations.lands: the atolls and islands of the Republic of the Marshall Islands, including Majuro

facts.text: Waan Aelõñ in Majel, Canoes of the Marshall Islands, is a Majuro program that trains young Marshallese women and men in skills for a sustainable future.

source.title: Canoes of the Marshall Islands, Waan Aelõñ in Majel

facts.text: In the Waan Aelõñ in Majel program, stick charts are still key tools for training new navigators in Marshallese wayfinding.

source.title: Canoes of the Marshall Islands, Waan Aelõñ in Majel

nations.name: Meriam
nations.lands: Mer (Murray Island) and nearby islands in the eastern Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia

facts.text: Meriam Mir is the traditional language of Mer, an island in the far east of the Torres Strait from which the Great Barrier Reef can be seen.

source.title: Murray Island - Mer Eruer Uteb
source.publisher: Tagai State College (Queensland Department of Education)

nations.name: Moriori
nations.lands: Rēkohu and Rangihaute (the Chatham and Pitt Islands), Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Moriori are the Indigenous people of Rēkohu and Rangihaute, the Chatham Islands, and are represented by the Hokotehi Moriori Trust.
The Hokotehi Moriori Trust takes part in key parts of the Rēkohu economy, such as fishing, farming and tourism.

nations.name: Nauruans
nations.lands: the island of Nauru, officially styled Naoero, in the central Pacific

facts.text: Nauru's government now presents the country as the Republic of Naoero on its official website.

source.title: The Government of the Republic of Naoero
source.publisher: Government of the Republic of Nauru

facts.text: In Nauru's 2021 census, 69 percent of residents aged 5 and over spoke only Nauruan at home, and another 25.3 percent spoke it with another language.

source.title: Nauru 2021 Population and Housing Census: Analytical Report

nations.name: Ngāi Tahu
nations.lands: Te Waipounamu (the South Island), Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: There are 18 Papatipu Rūnanga, local Ngāi Tahu councils, spread throughout Te Waipounamu, the South Island.

source.title: Ngāi Tahu | Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu

facts.text: Ngāi Tahu means people of Tahu, and whakapapa, the ancestral link, binds all Ngāi Tahu whānau.

source.title: Ngāi Tahu | Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu

nations.name: Ngāi Tūhoe
nations.lands: Te Urewera, in the eastern North Island, Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: A Treaty settlement signed in 2013 provided for Te Urewera, the Tūhoe homeland, to have its own law and a separate legal identity, governed by Tūhoe and Crown nominees.

source.title: Ngāi Tūhoe
source.publisher: Te Kāhui Whakatau (Treaty Settlements), New Zealand Government

facts.text: Tūhoe had about 9,300 registered members at the time of their 2013 Treaty settlement.

source.title: Ngāi Tūhoe
source.publisher: Te Kāhui Whakatau (Treaty Settlements), New Zealand Government

nations.name: Ngāti Porou
nations.lands: Te Tairāwhiti, the East Coast of the North Island, from Pōtikirua to Te Toka-a-Taiau, Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Ngāti Porou's tribal area runs down Te Tairāwhiti, between Pōtikirua (Lottin Point) in the north and Te Toka-a-Taiau in the south.
The Ngāti Porou pepeha names Hikurangi as their mountain and Waiapu as their river.

nations.name: Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei
nations.lands: Central Tāmaki Makaurau (Auckland), Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei's shared affairs are looked after by their Trust and two subsidiaries: Whai Māia, the social arm, and Whai Rawa, the commercial arm.
Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei are the tangata whenua, the people of the land, of Te Kahu Tōpuni o Tuperiri in central Tāmaki Makaurau (Auckland).

nations.name: ni-Vanuatu
nations.lands: the islands of the Republic of Vanuatu in the south-west Pacific, including Malakula and the central and northern islands

facts.text: Vanuatu Cultural Centre fieldworkers, or filwokas, are volunteers nominated by their communities across the islands to promote, protect and preserve kastom.

source.title: Grassroots Badly Burnt: the loss of ni-Vanuatu archaeologists whose careers spanned 50 years

facts.text: In 1998 Na'hai speakers of south Malakula opened the Na'hai Kaljaral Senta, the first language-based cultural centre in Vanuatu.

source.title: Kastom as Development: Opening the Na'hai Kaljaral Senta

nations.name: Niueans
nations.lands: the island of Niue in the South Pacific, with villages such as Alofi, Mutalau and Toi

facts.text: Fale Tāoga Niue, home of the Niue National Museum, opened on 19 October 2018, the anniversary of the Niue Constitution Celebrations.
Niue's Vagahau Niue Act 2012 recognises Vagahau Niue as the official language of Niue and created the Niue Language Commission to protect it.

source.title: Vagahau Niue Act 2012
source.publisher: Université Laval, CEFAN: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde

nations.name: Noongar
nations.lands: The south-west of Western Australia, including the Perth region, Australia

facts.text: Western Australia's settlement recognises the Noongar people as the traditional owners of the South-West, with about A$1.3 billion in land and other benefits.

source.title: All six South West Native Title Settlement Agreements registered

facts.text: The South West Native Title Settlement covers about 200,000 square kilometres and affects an estimated 40,000 Noongar people.

source.title: South West Aboriginal Land and Sea Council
source.publisher: South West Aboriginal Land and Sea Council

nations.name: Palauans
nations.lands: the Republic of Palau in the western Pacific, with 16 states on Babeldaob, Koror and other islands

facts.text: Palauans still use the Rock Islands Southern Lagoon, a World Heritage site since 2012, for cultural purposes under a traditional governance system.
Palau's Council of Chiefs, made up of the highest traditional chiefs from each state, advises the President on traditional laws and customs.

nations.name: Papuan peoples
nations.lands: The Papua region of Indonesia, the western half of the island of New Guinea

facts.text: Men and women in Papua use the noken to carry garden produce, and it may also be worn at festivities or given as a peace offering.

source.title: Noken multifunctional knotted or woven bag, handcraft of the people of Papua

facts.text: The noken, a bag that communities in Papua knot or weave by hand from wood fibre or leaves, was inscribed on a UNESCO list for urgent safeguarding in 2012.

source.title: Noken multifunctional knotted or woven bag, handcraft of the people of Papua

nations.name: Pohnpeians
nations.lands: Pohnpei State in the Federated States of Micronesia, on Pohnpei island and its outlying atolls

facts.text: Nan Madol, a World Heritage site since 2016, is traditionally owned and managed under the Nahnmwarki system, a chiefly institution that continues in Pohnpei today.

source.title: Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia

facts.text: Pohnpei State's constitution protects the customs and traditions of Pohnpei's traditional kingdoms alongside its elected government.

source.title: Pohnpei
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

nations.name: Rapa Nui
nations.lands: Rapa Nui (Easter Island), in the south-eastern Pacific, Chile

facts.text: Tapati Rapa Nui, the island's main cultural festival, filled two weeks of February 2026 with ancestral competitions, arts and celebrations of Rapa Nui identity, language and traditions.

source.title: Ministra de las Culturas participa en inauguración de la Tapati Rapanui y desarrolla agenda de trabajo en la isla
source.publisher: Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio (Chile)

facts.text: In 2017, 642 votes were cast in a formal consultation with the Rapa Nui people on a marine protected area for their island, and yes won all three questions.

source.title: Informe del Proceso de Consulta al pueblo Rapa Nui sobre creación, administración y regulación de usos de un Área Marina Costera Protegida de Múltiples Usos para Rapa Nui
source.publisher: Ministerio del Medio Ambiente, Gobierno de Chile

nations.name: Refaluwasch
nations.lands: Saipan and other islands of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, a United States commonwealth in the western Pacific

facts.text: In December 2020 the Matawal Wóól Display Hall opened with photos and crafts made by students of the Tepengi Kkosch Refaluwasch culture program.

source.title: Carolinian Affairs Office 2021 Citizen Centric Report

facts.text: The Carolinian Affairs Office, created by the CNMI Constitution, advises the governor and works to protect and preserve the culture and traditions of Indigenous Carolinians.

source.title: Carolinian Affairs Office 2020 Citizen Centric Report

nations.name: Rotumans
nations.lands: the island of Rotuma and its islets, about 500 km north of Fiji's main islands, and communities across Fiji

facts.text: Rotuma is divided into seven districts, each led by a district chief, the gagaj 'es itu'u, with village groups called ho'aga under their own chiefs.

source.title: Hierarchy (Kato'aga: Rotuman Ceremonies)
source.publisher: The Rotuma Website, University of Hawai'i

facts.text: Rotumans are a distinct people with their own language, Fäeag Rotuạm, which New Zealand celebrates each year in Rotuman Language Week.

source.title: Gasav Ne Fäeag Rotuạm Ta: Rotuman Language Week

nations.name: Samoans
nations.lands: the Independent State of Samoa, on Upolu, Savai'i and nearby islands

facts.text: Women and master weavers have formed fine mat committees in their villages, and more young women, and some men, now weave the 'ie Samoa.

source.title: 'Ie Samoa, fine mat and its cultural value

facts.text: Samoa's 2021 census counted 16,082 people aged 21 and over who hold a matai, or chiefly, title, including 1,444 women.

source.title: Samoa Population and Housing Census 2021 Fact Sheet (Final Results, October 2022)

nations.name: Te Arawa
nations.lands: Rotorua and the Rotorua lakes district, Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Rotorua was declared New Zealand's first bilingual district in 2017, and the council has since worked with Te Tatau o Te Arawa on changes like bilingual road signs.
The Te Arawa Lakes settlement, signed in 2004, provided for title to 13 lakebeds to be returned to Te Arawa, a large confederation of iwi and hapū.

source.title: Te Arawa Lakes
source.publisher: Te Kāhui Whakatau (Treaty Settlements), New Zealand Government

nations.name: Tiwi
nations.lands: The Tiwi Islands (Bathurst and Melville Islands), about 80 km north of Darwin in the Arafura Sea, Northern Territory, Australia

facts.text: There are eight landowning groups on the Tiwi Islands, and Tiwi people have an unbroken history of occupying and owning their islands.
The Tiwi Islands, about 80 km north of Darwin, are home to just over 3,000 people, more than 90 percent of them Tiwi.

nations.name: Tokelauans
nations.lands: the three atolls of Tokelau, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, in the South Pacific

facts.text: In Tokelau the Taupulega, the village councils of elders, remain the ultimate source of authority, and they grant the General Fono its powers.
The role of Ulu-o-Tokelau, head of the national government, rotates each year among the elected leaders of Tokelau's three atolls.

nations.name: Tongans
nations.lands: the Kingdom of Tonga in the South Pacific, including Tongatapu, Vava'u, Ha'apai, 'Eua and the Niuas

facts.text: Tonga's 2021 census counted 100,179 people in the kingdom, a young population with a median age of 19 for males and 22 for females.
Lakalaka, often called Tonga's national dance, joins choreography, oratory and sung polyphony, and is performed at coronations and constitution anniversaries.

source.title: Lakalaka, dances and sung speeches of Tonga

nations.name: Torres Strait Islanders
nations.lands: the islands of the Torres Strait between Cape York and Papua New Guinea, in Queensland, Australia, and the Northern Peninsula Area

facts.text: The Torres Strait Regional Authority, an Australian Government body set up on 1 July 1994, counts recognising and maintaining Torres Strait Islander Ailan Kastom among its functions.
Kala Lagaw Ya is the traditional language of the western and central Torres Strait islands, and Meriam Mir is the language of the eastern islands.

nations.name: Tuvaluans
nations.lands: the nine islands of Tuvalu in the central Pacific, including Funafuti

facts.text: Each island in Tuvalu has a falekaupule, a traditional assembly of elders also called te sina o fenua, the grey-hairs of the land.

source.title: The Local Government System in Tuvalu

facts.text: Tuvaluan has eight dialects from eight of the islands, and the name Tuvalu joins tu, to stand, with valu, eight.

source.title: Tuvalu language activity book
source.publisher: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

nations.name: Waikato-Tainui
nations.lands: The Waikato region of the North Island, Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Waikato-Tainui describes itself as a growing tribe of over 90,000 people, voyagers and pioneers like their ancestors.

source.title: Ko Waikato te iwi, ko Tainui te waka

facts.text: Waikato-Tainui celebrate their identity as people of the Tainui waka and as protectors of the Kiingitanga movement.

source.title: Ko Waikato te iwi, ko Tainui te waka

nations.name: Whanganui Iwi
nations.lands: The Whanganui River, from the mountains to the sea, North Island, Aotearoa New Zealand

facts.text: Ngā Tāngata Tiaki o Whanganui, the iwi river trust, was established in August 2014 with the signing of Ruruku Whakatupua.

source.title: Home | Ngā Tāngata Tiaki o Whanganui

facts.text: Since 2017, New Zealand law has recognised the Whanganui River, Te Awa Tupua, as a legal person, with a guardian office that acts as its human face.

source.title: The Whanganui River (Te Awa Tupua)
source.publisher: OsloMet (Oslo Metropolitan University), River Rights project

nations.name: Wiradjuri
nations.lands: Central New South Wales, the country of the Wambool (Macquarie), Kalari (Lachlan) and Murrumbidjeri (Murrumbidgee) rivers, Australia

facts.text: A Charles Sturt University course shaped by Wiradjuri Elders works to build a living community of Wiradjuri speakers; it won a 2019 MacJannet Prize.

source.title: The Graduate Certificate in Wiradjuri Language Culture and Heritage, Charles Sturt University (Australia)
source.publisher: Talloires Network of Engaged Universities (Tufts University)

facts.text: Wiradjuri people were known as the people of the three rivers: the Wambool (Macquarie), the Kalari (Lachlan) and the Murrumbidjeri (Murrumbidgee).

nations.name: Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung
nations.lands: Melbourne and surrounding lands, including the Birrarung (Yarra River), Victoria, Australia

facts.text: The Wurundjeri council was set up in 1985 by Wurundjeri descendants and gained Registered Aboriginal Party status for cultural heritage in 2008.

source.title: Recent Past & Present
source.publisher: Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation

facts.text: In 2017 a Yarra River protection bill was the first legislation put before Victoria's parliament with a dual Aboriginal language title: Wilip-gin Birrarung murron, keep the Birrarung alive.

source.title: Recent Past & Present
source.publisher: Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation

nations.name: Yapese
nations.lands: the main islands of Yap (Yap, Gagil, Tomil and Rumung) in Yap State, Federated States of Micronesia

facts.text: Yap's state constitution creates the Council of Pilung and the Council of Tamol, councils of traditional leaders whose work concerns tradition and custom.

source.title: Yap State Code, Title 5: Traditional Leaders and Traditions
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

facts.text: Under Yap State law the two councils advise the Governor and Legislature and work to promote and preserve the traditions and customs of the people.

Once at risk of disappearing, Chinuk Wawa is growing again and is actively taught and used in Grand Ronde cultural education.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians
nations.lands: Siletz, on the central Oregon coast; ancestral territory across western Oregon into southwest Washington and northern California

facts.text: After lobbying Congress, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians won repeal of federal termination in 1977.
The Tribe's Athabaskan language dictionary, Nuu-wee-ya' (Our words), holds about 12,000 entries, and a Talking Dictionary lets learners hear words spoken aloud.

source.title: Language - Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
nations.lands: Umatilla Indian Reservation in northeastern Oregon, home of the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla peoples

facts.text: CTUIR teaches the Umatilla, Walla Walla and Weyíiletpuu (Cayuse) languages to all ages, drawing on the knowledge of fluent speakers.

source.title: Languages of the CTUIR
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

facts.text: Nixyáawii, the homeland name used by the Tribes' language program, means the place of many springs.

source.title: Languages of the CTUIR
source.publisher: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs
nations.lands: Central Oregon, stretching east from the summit of the Cascade Mountains

facts.text: The Museum at Warm Springs shares the history and culture of the three tribes and welcomes visitors in Ichishkiin, Numu and Kiksht.

source.title: Museum at Warm Springs - Culture. History. In Living Color.

facts.text: In 1937 the Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute organized as one confederated government under their own constitution and bylaws.

nations.name: Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria
nations.lands: Sonoma and Marin counties, California, with a reservation near Rohnert Park

facts.text: Graton Rancheria launched its own Tribal TANF program serving low-income Native American families in Sonoma and Marin counties.
Graton Rancheria, a federation of Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo groups, regained federal recognition through a law signed on December 27, 2000.

nations.name: Hoopa Valley Tribe
nations.lands: Hoopa Valley along the Trinity River, Humboldt County, northern California

facts.text: The Hoopa Valley Tribe runs its own Fisheries Department, which counts the harvest and spawning returns of salmon, steelhead, sturgeon and lamprey.
Tribal fisheries crews made major progress restoring the lower reaches of Supply Creek and Mill Creek between 2015 and 2018.

nations.name: Karuk Tribe
nations.lands: Klamath River country of northern California, with tribal offices in Happy Camp

facts.text: The Karuk Language Program teaches all ages through community classes, school partnerships and immersion, linking learners with fluent speakers.
The Karuk People's Center in Happy Camp opened in September 2002 and holds a museum, library, basketweaving classroom and the language program office.

nations.name: Kashia Band of Pomo Indians
also: Kashia Band of Pomo Indians of the Stewarts Point Rancheria
nations.lands: Sonoma County coast of California, from the Gualala River south toward the Russian River

facts.text: The Kashia Band owns the 688-acre Kashia Coastal Reserve, which spans both sides of Highway 1 just north of Salt Point State Park.
Kashia homelands reached from the Gualala River in the north to Duncan's Point, south of the Russian River.

nations.name: Lummi Nation
nations.lands: Northernmost coast of Washington State and the waters of Puget Sound, with ancestral lands reaching into southern British Columbia

facts.text: Northwest Indian College, with its main campus on the Lummi Reservation, is the only accredited tribal college serving Washington, Oregon and Idaho.

source.title: About | Northwest Indian College | Accredited Tribal College

facts.text: The Lhaq'temish, the Lummi People, describe themselves as fishers, hunters, gatherers and harvesters of the Puget Sound shores and waters.

nations.name: Makah Tribe
nations.lands: Neah Bay and Cape Flattery, at the northwest tip of Washington's Olympic Peninsula

facts.text: The name Makah came from neighboring tribes and means people generous with food.
The Makah Reservation at Neah Bay sits on the northwest tip of the continental United States.

nations.name: Morongo Band of Mission Indians
nations.lands: Morongo Indian Reservation beneath the San Gorgonio Mountains, Riverside County, California

facts.text: Morongo tribal members elect a seven-member Tribal Council to lead their independent tribal government.
Established in 1865, the Morongo Indian Reservation now spans more than 35,000 acres.

nations.name: Muckleshoot Indian Tribe
nations.lands: South King County, Washington, in the Puget Sound region; ancestors include Duwamish and Upper Puyallup peoples

facts.text: The Muckleshoot Indian Tribe is one of South King County's largest employers, supporting about 3,300 direct jobs.
Among Puget Sound tribes, Muckleshoot is the only one holding rights under two treaties.

nations.name: Nimiipuu
nations.lands: North-central Idaho, with homelands across present-day Idaho, Washington, Oregon and Montana

facts.text: Nimipuutímt, the Nez Perce language, is a core part of Nimiipuu culture.
Headquartered in Lapwai, Idaho, the Nez Perce Reservation spans about 770,000 acres.

nations.name: Puyallup Tribe of Indians
nations.lands: Shores of southern Puget Sound and the Puyallup River, Tacoma area, Washington

facts.text: One of the most urban tribes in the United States, the Puyallup still fish, hunt and travel the waters of the Puyallup River.
The Tribe gives its name as puyaləpabš, meaning people at the bend at the bottom of the river.

nations.name: Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe
nations.lands: Pyramid Lake and its reservation, about 35 miles northeast of Reno, Nevada

facts.text: The Tribe's Language Program offers community Paiute classes, lessons inside schools and meetings with fluent speakers.
The reservation covers 475,000 acres around Pyramid Lake, which runs about 27 miles long and 11 miles wide.

nations.name: Quinault Indian Nation
nations.lands: Southwestern corner of Washington's Olympic Peninsula, between the Olympic Mountains and the Pacific Ocean

facts.text: The Nation has a Taholah Village Relocation Master Plan that includes planning for an upper village, and its Planning Department is updating the plan for 2026.

source.title: Taholah Village Relocation | Quinault Indian Nation, WA

facts.text: The Quinault Language Department works to revitalize the Quinault language, with in-person classes in Taholah, Queets and Hoquiam.

source.title: Language Department | Quinault Indian Nation, WA

nations.name: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians
nations.lands: Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Barbara County, California

facts.text: The Tribe's Culture Department founded its language program in 2008, and the Tribe has unveiled a Samala-English Dictionary.

source.title: Culture
source.publisher: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians

facts.text: Established on December 27, 1901, the Santa Ynez Reservation began with 99 acres and has grown to more than 1,500 acres.

source.title: The Santa Ynez Reservation
source.publisher: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians

nations.name: Swinomish Indian Tribal Community
nations.lands: Swinomish Reservation near La Conner, Skagit County, Washington

facts.text: The Swinomish Tribe monitors air quality in partnership with the EPA, with two major oil refineries right next to its reservation.
Swinomish monitors record real-time data on particulates, ozone and nitrogen dioxide, plus weather such as wind, temperature, humidity and precipitation.

nations.name: Te-Moak Tribe of Western Shoshone Indians
nations.lands: Northeastern Nevada, in Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells

facts.text: The Te-Moak Tribe unites four bands, Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells, under one tribal council elected every three years.
Western Shoshone people are descendants of an ancient, widespread people whose name, Newe, means The People.

nations.name: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe
nations.lands: Death Valley and surrounding areas of California and Nevada

facts.text: Today the federally recognized Timbisha Shoshone Tribe works to keep its language, traditions and sovereignty strong.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

facts.text: The Timbisha, part of the larger Western Shoshone people, have lived in Death Valley and its surrounding areas for thousands of years, and their village sits inside Death Valley National Park.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

nations.name: Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation
nations.lands: Smith River and the coast of Del Norte County, far northern California

facts.text: The Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation was restored in 1983 through a court case, and its restored government extended citizenship to all Taa-laa-wa Dee-ni'.
Tolowa Dee-ni' language work goes back to a language program formed in 1969, and the Nation calls revitalization vital to Tolowa identity.

nations.name: Tongva
nations.lands: Greater Los Angeles region of California, a homeland called Tovaangar

facts.text: The conservancy, a Tongva-led nonprofit and not a tribal government, serves Tongva people, the wider Native community and guests, called kuuyam.
In 2022 Huhuunga, a one-acre parcel in Altadena, was returned to Tongva stewardship. It is now home to the Tongva-led Tongva Taraxat Paxaavxa Conservancy.

nations.name: Tulalip Tribes
nations.lands: Tulalip Indian Reservation on Puget Sound, Snohomish County, Washington

facts.text: The Tulalip Lushootseed Language Department works toward every tribal home, workplace, gathering and classroom being rich in Lushootseed.
The Tulalip Tribes count over 5,100 people, about 2,700 of whom live on the 22,000-acre Tulalip Indian Reservation.

nations.name: Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians
nations.lands: Sierra Nevada foothills, Tuolumne County, California

facts.text: In January 2005 the Tribe opened the Tuolumne Me-Wuk Indian Health Center.

source.title: History - The Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians

facts.text: Tuolumne Rancheria began in 1910 with 289.52 acres; today the Tribe holds more than 1,700 acres of fee and trust land.

source.title: History - The Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians

nations.name: Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians
nations.lands: Viejas Reservation in the mountains east of San Diego, California; the wider Kumeyaay homeland reaches into Baja California, Mexico

facts.text: Viejas extends its community work beyond San Diego to Kumeyaay relatives in Baja California, Mexico.
Viejas government rests on participatory democracy, with tribal officials elected by the general council to four-year terms.

nations.name: Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California
nations.lands: Lake Tahoe region and nearby valleys of western Nevada and eastern California

facts.text: Washoe teachers hold language classes for adults and youth four days a week, and immersion classes reach children in the tribe's Head Start.

source.title: Where Wašiw is Spoken: The Washoe Tribe is Passing Its Unique Language On and Up
source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (American Indian magazine)

facts.text: The name Tahoe is thought to come from Da ow ga, the Washoe word for lake.

source.title: Discover History
source.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit

nations.name: Yurok Tribe
nations.lands: Lower Klamath River and the Pacific coast of far northern California, United States

facts.text: When Yurok people speak of themselves, they say Oohl, which means Indian people.
On June 30, 2026, Save the Redwoods League conveyed 125 acres on Prairie Creek, in the heart of Yurok ancestral territory, back to the Yurok Tribe.
